Verified Uncertainty Calibration

Ananya Kumar Affiliation: Department of Computer Science    Percy Liang Affiliation: Stanford University    Tengyu Ma Affiliation: {ananya, pliang, tengyuma}@cs.stanford.edu
Abstract

Applications such as weather forecasting and personalized medicine demand models that output calibrated probability estimates—those representative of the true likelihood of a prediction. Most models are not calibrated out of the box but are recalibrated by post-processing model outputs. We find in this work that popular recalibration methods like Platt scaling and temperature scaling are (i) less calibrated than reported, and (ii) current techniques cannot estimate how miscalibrated they are. An alternative method, histogram binning, has measurable calibration error but is sample inefficient—it requires O⁡(B/ϵ2)O(B/\epsilon^{2}) samples, compared to O⁡(1/ϵ2)O(1/\epsilon^{2}) for scaling methods, where BB is the number of distinct probabilities the model can output. To get the best of both worlds, we introduce the scaling-binning calibrator, which first fits a parametric function to reduce variance and then bins the function values to actually ensure calibration. This requires only O⁡(1/ϵ2+B)O(1/\epsilon^{2}+B) samples. Next, we show that we can estimate a model’s calibration error more accurately using an estimator from the meteorological community—or equivalently measure its calibration error with fewer samples (O⁡(B)O(\sqrt{B}) instead of O⁡(B)O(B)). We validate our approach with multiclass calibration experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, where we obtain a 35% lower calibration error than histogram binning and, unlike scaling methods, guarantees on true calibration. In these experiments, we also estimate the calibration error and ECE more accurately than the commonly used plugin estimators. We implement all these methods in a Python library: https://pypi.org/project/uncertainty-calibration

1 Introduction

The probability that a system outputs for an event should reflect the true frequency of that event: if an automated diagnosis system says 1,000 patients have cancer with probability 0.1, approximately 100 of them should indeed have cancer. In this case, we say the model is uncertainty calibrated. The importance of this notion of calibration has been emphasized in personalized medicine [1], meteorological forecasting [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] and natural language processing applications [7, 8]. As most modern machine learning models, such as neural networks, do not output calibrated probabilities out of the box [9, 10, 11], reseachers use recalibration methods that take the output of an uncalibrated model, and transform it into a calibrated probability. Scaling approaches for recalibration—Platt scaling [12], isotonic regression [13], and temperature scaling [9]—are widely used and require very few samples, but do they actually produce calibrated probabilities?

We discover that these methods are less calibrated than reported. Past work approximates a model’s calibration error using a finite set of bins. We show that by using more bins, we can uncover a higher calibration error for models on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. We show that a fundamental limitation with approaches that output a continuous range of probabilities is that their true calibration error is unmeasurable with a finite number of bins (Example 3.2).

An alternative approach, histogram binning [10], outputs probabilities from a finite set. Histogram binning can produce a model that is calibrated, and unlike scaling methods we can measure its calibration error, but it is sample inefficient. In particular, the number of samples required to calibrate scales linearly with the number of distinct probabilities the model can output, BB [14], which can be large particularly in the multiclass setting where BB typically scales with the number of classes. Recalibration sample efficiency is crucial—we often want to recalibrate our models in the presence of domain shift [15] or recalibrate a model trained on simulated data, and may have access to only a small labeled dataset from the target domain.

To get the sample efficiency of Platt scaling and the verification guarantees of histogram binning, we propose the scaling-binning calibrator (Figure 1(c)). Like scaling methods, we fit a simple function g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} to the recalibration dataset. We then bin the input space so that an equal number of inputs land in each bin. In each bin, we output the average of the gg values in that bin—these are the gray circles in Figure 1(c). In contrast, histogram binning outputs the average of the label values in each bin (Figure 1(b)). The motivation behind our method is that the gg values in each bin are in a narrower range than the label values, so when we take the average we incur lower estimation error. If 𝒢\mathcal{G} is well chosen, our method requires O⁡(1ϵ2+B)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}+B) samples to achieve calibration error ϵ\epsilon instead of O⁡(Bϵ2)O(\frac{B}{\epsilon^{2}}) samples for histogram binning, where BB is the number of model outputs (Theorem 4.1). Note that in prior work, binning the outputs of a function was used for evaluation and without any guarantees, whereas in our case it is used for the method itself, and we show improved sample complexity.

We run multiclass calibration experiments on CIFAR-10 [20] and ImageNet [21]. The scaling-binning calibrator achieves a lower calibration error than histogram binning, while allowing us to measure the true calibration error unlike for scaling methods. We get a 35% lower calibration error on CIFAR-10 and a 5x lower calibration error on ImageNet than histogram binning for B=100B=100.

Finally, we show how to estimate the calibration error of models more accurately. Prior work in machine learning [7, 9, 15, 16, 17] directly estimates each term in the calibration error from samples (Definition 5.1). The sample complexity of this plugin estimator scales linearly with BB. A debiased estimator introduced in the meteorological literature [18, 19] reduces the bias of the plugin estimator; we prove that it achieves sample complexity that scales with B\sqrt{B} by leveraging error cancellations across bins. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet confirm that the debiased estimator measures the calibration error more accurately.

2 Setup and background

2.1 Binary classification

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the input space and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be the label space where 𝒴={0,1}\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1\} for binary classification. Let X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} and Y∈𝒴Y\in\mathcal{Y} be random variables denoting the input and label, given by an unknown joint distribution PP. As usual, expectations are taken over all random variables.

Suppose we have a model f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] where the (possibly uncalibrated) output of the model represents the model’s confidence that the label is 1. The calibration error examines the difference between the model’s probability and the true probability given the model’s output:

Definition 2.1 (Calibration error).

The calibration error of f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] is given by:

CE​(f)=(𝔼[|f⁡(X)−𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)]|2])1/2\displaystyle\textup{CE}(f)=\Big(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\big[\left|f(X)-\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)]\right|^{2}\big]\Big)^{1/2} (1)

If CE​(f)=0\textup{CE}(f)=0 then ff is perfectly calibrated. This notion of calibration error is most commonly used [2, 3, 4, 7, 15, 16, 17, 18]. Replacing the 22s in the above definition by p≥1p\geq 1 we get the ℓp\ell_{p} calibration error—the ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} calibration errors are also used in the literature [9, 23, 24]. In addition to CE, we also deal with the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error (known as ECE) in Sections 3 and 5.

Calibration alone is not sufficient: consider an image dataset containing 50%50\% dogs and 50%50\% cats. If ff outputs 0.50.5 on all inputs, ff is calibrated but not very useful. We often also wish to minimize the mean-squared error—also known as the Brier score—subject to a calibration budget [5, 25].

Definition 2.2.

The mean-squared error of f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] is given by MSE​(f)=𝔼⁡[(f⁡(X)−Y)2]\textup{MSE}(f)=\mathbb{E}[(f(X)-Y)^{2}].

Note that MSE and CE are not orthogonal and MSE=0\mbox{MSE}=0 implies perfect calibration; in fact the MSE is the sum of the squared calibration error and a “sharpness” term [2, 4, 16].

2.2 Multiclass classification

While calibration in binary classification is well-studied, it’s less clear what to do for multiclass, where multiple definitions abound, differing in their strengths. In the multiclass setting, 𝒴=[K]={1,…,K}\mathcal{Y}=[K]=\{1,\dots,K\} and f:𝒳→[0,1]Kf:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]^{K} outputs a confidence measure for each class in [K][K].

Definition 2.3 (Top-label calibration error).

The top-label calibration error examines the difference between the model’s probability for its top prediction and the true probability of that prediction given the model’s output:

TCE​(f)=(𝔼[(ℙ⁡(Y=arg​maxj∈[K]⁡f​(X)j∣maxj∈[K]⁡f​(X)j)−maxj∈[K]⁡f​(X)j)2])1/2\displaystyle\textup{TCE}(f)=\Big(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\Big(\mathbb{P}\big(Y=\argmax_{j\in[K]}f(X)_{j}\mid\max_{j\in[K]}f(X)_{j}\big)-\max_{j\in[K]}f(X)_{j}\Big)^{2}\Big]\Big)^{1/2} (2)

We would often like the model to be calibrated on less likely predictions as well—imagine that a medical diagnosis system says there is a 50%50\% chance a patient has a benign tumor, a 10%10\% chance she has an aggressive form of cancer, and a 40%40\% chance she has one of a long list of other conditions. We would like the model to be calibrated on all of these predictions so we define the marginal calibration error which examines, for each class, the difference between the model’s probability and the true probability of that class given the model’s output.

Definition 2.4 (Marginal calibration error).

Let wk∈[0,1]w_{k}\in[0,1] denote how important calibrating class kk is, where wk=1/kw_{k}=1/k if all classes are equally important. The marginal calibration error is:

MCE​(f)=(∑k=1Kwk​𝔼​[(f​(X)k−ℙ⁡(Y=k∣f​(X)k))2])1/2\displaystyle\textup{MCE}(f)=\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\mathbb{E}\big[(f(X)_{k}-\mathbb{P}(Y=k\mid f(X)_{k}))^{2}\big]\Big)^{1/2} (3)

Prior works [9, 15, 17] propose methods for multiclass calibration but only measure top-label calibration—[24] and concurrent work to ours [26] define similar per-class calibration metrics where temperature scaling [9] is worse than vector scaling despite having better top-label calibration.

For notational simplicity, our theory focuses on the binary classification setting. We can transform top-label calibration into a binary calibration problem—the model outputs a probability corresponding to its top prediction, and the label represents whether the model gets it correct or not. Marginal calibration can be transformed into KK one-vs-all binary calibration problems where for each k∈[K]k\in[K] the model outputs the probability associated with the kk-th class, and the label represents whether the correct class is kk [13]. We consider both top-label calibration and marginal calibration in our experiments. Other notions of multiclass calibration include joint calibration (which requires the entire probability vector to be calibrated) [2, 6] and event-pooled calibration [16].

2.3 Recalibration

Since most machine learning models do not output calibrated probabilities out of the box [9, 10] recalibration methods take the output of an uncalibrated model, and transform it into a calibrated probability. That is, given a trained model f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1], let Z=f⁡(X)Z=f(X). We are given recalibration data T={(zi,yi)}i=1nT=\{(z_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} independently sampled from P⁡(Z,Y)P(Z,Y), and we wish to learn a recalibrator g:[0,1]→[0,1]g:[0,1]\to[0,1] such that g∘fg\circ f is well-calibrated.

Scaling methods, for example Platt scaling [12], output a function g=arg​ming∈𝒢∑(z,y)∈Tℓ(g(z),y)g=\argmin_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{(z,y)\in T}\ell(g(z),y), where 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a model family, g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} is differentiable, and ℓ\ell is a loss function, for example the log-loss or mean-squared error. The advantage of such methods is that they converge very quickly since they only fit a small number of parameters.

Histogram binning first constructs a set of bins (intervals) that partitions [0,1][0,1], formalized below.

Definition 2.5 (Binning schemes).

A binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B} of size BB is a set of BB intervals I1,…,IBI_{1},\dots,I_{B} that partitions [0,1][0,1]. Given z∈[0,1]z\in[0,1], let β⁡(z)=j\beta(z)=j, where jj is the interval that zz lands in (z∈Ijz\in I_{j}).

The bins are typically chosen such that either I1=[0,1B],I2=(1B,2B],…,IB=(B−1B,1]I_{1}=[0,\frac{1}{B}],I_{2}=(\frac{1}{B},\frac{2}{B}],\dots,I_{B}=(\frac{B-1}{B},1] (equal width binning) [9] or so that each bin contains an equal number of ziz_{i} values in the recalibration data (uniform mass binning) [10]. Histogram binning then outputs the average yiy_{i} value in each bin.

3 Is Platt scaling calibrated?

In this section, we show that methods like Platt scaling and temperature scaling are (i) less calibrated than reported and (ii) it is difficult to tell how miscalibrated they are. That is we show, both theoretically and with experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, why the calibration error of models that output a continuous range of values is underestimated. We defer proofs to Appendix B.

The key to estimating the calibration error is estimating the conditional expectation 𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)]. If f⁡(X)f(X) is continuous, without smoothness assumptions on 𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)] (that cannot be verified in practice), this is impossible. This is analogous to the difficulty of measuring the mutual information between two continuous signals [27].

To approximate the calibration error, prior work bins the output of ff into BB intervals. The calibration error in each bin is estimated as the difference between the average value of f⁡(X)f(X) and YY in that bin. Note that the binning here is for evaluation only, whereas in histogram binning, it is used for the recalibration method itself. We formalize the notion of this binned calibration error below.

Definition 3.1.

The binned version of ff outputs the average value of ff in each bin IjI_{j}:

fℬ​(x)=𝔼[f⁡(X)∣f⁡(X)∈Ij]where ​x∈Ij\displaystyle f_{\mathcal{B}}(x)=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[f(X)\mid f(X)\in I_{j}]\quad\quad\quad\mbox{where }x\in I_{j} (4)

Given ℬ\mathcal{B}{}, the binned calibration error of ff is simply the calibration error of fℬf_{\mathcal{B}{}}. A simple example shows that using binning to estimate the calibration error can severely underestimate the true calibration error.

Example 3.2.

For any binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{}, and continuous bijective function f:[0,1]→[0,1]f:[0,1]\to[0,1], there exists a distribution PP over 𝒳,𝒴\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} s.t. CE​(fℬ)=0\textup{CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}})=0 but CE​(f)≥0.49\textup{CE}(f)\geq 0.49. Note that for all ff, 0≤CE​(f)≤10\leq\textup{CE}(f)\leq 1.

The intuition of the construction is that in each interval IjI_{j} in ℬ\mathcal{B}{}, the model could underestimate the true probability 𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)] half the time, and overestimate the probability half the time. So if we average over the entire bin the model appears to be calibrated, even though it is very uncalibrated. The formal proof is in Appendix B, and holds for arbitrary ℓp\ell_{p} calibration errors including the ECE.

Next, we show that given a function ff, its binned version always has lower calibration error. The proof, in Appendix B, is by Jensen’s inequality. Intuitively, averaging a model’s prediction within a bin allows errors at different parts of the bin to cancel out with each other. This result is similar to Theorem 2 in recent work [28], and holds for arbitrary ℓp\ell_{p} calibration errors including the ECE.

Proposition 3.3 (Binning underestimates error).

Given any binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{} and model f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1], we have:

CE​(fℬ)≤CE​(f).\textup{CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}})\leq\textup{CE}(f).

3.1 Experiments

Our experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 suggest that previous work reports numbers which are lower than the actual calibration error of their models. Recall that binning lower bounds the calibration error. We cannot compute the actual calibration error but if we use a ‘finer’ set of bins then we get a tighter lower bound on the calibration error.

As in [9], our model’s objective was to output the top predicted class and a confidence score associated with the prediction. For ImageNet, we started with a trained VGG16 model with an accuracy of 64.3%. We split the validation set into 3 sets of sizes (20000,5000,25000)(20000,5000,25000). We used the first set of data to recalibrate the model using Platt scaling, the second to select the binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B} so that each bin contains an equal number of points, and the third to measure the binned calibration error . We calculated 90%90\% confidence intervals for the binned calibration error using 1,000 bootstrap resamples and performed the same experiment with varying numbers of bins.

Figure 2(a) shows that as we increase the number of bins on ImageNet, the measured calibration error is higher and this is statistically significant. For example, if we use 15 bins as in [9], we would think the calibration error is around 0.02 when in reality the calibration error is at least twice as high. Figure 2(b) shows similar findings for CIFAR-10, and in Appendix C we show that our findings hold even if we use the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error (ECE) and alternative binning strategies.

4 The scaling-binning calibrator

Section 3 shows that the problem with scaling methods is we cannot estimate their calibration error. The upside of scaling methods is that if the function family has at least one function that can achieve calibration error ϵ\epsilon, they require O⁡(1/ϵ2)O(1/\epsilon^{2}) samples to reach calibration error ϵ\epsilon, while histogram binning requires O⁡(B/ϵ2)O(B/\epsilon^{2}) samples. Can we devise a method that is sample efficient to calibrate and one where it’s possible to estimate the calibration error? To achieve this, we propose the scaling-binning calibrator (Figure 1(c)) where we first fit a scaling function, and then bin the outputs of the scaling function.

4.1 Algorithm

We split the recalibration data TT of size nn into 3 sets: T1T_{1}, T2T_{2}, T3T_{3}. The scaling-binning calibrator, illustrated in Figure 1, outputs gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}}} such that gℬ^∘f\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}}}\circ f has low calibration error:

Step 1 (Function fitting): Select g=arg​ming∈𝒢∑(z,y)∈T1(y−g(z))2g=\argmin_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{(z,y)\in T_{1}}(y-g(z))^{2}.

Step 2 (Binning scheme construction): We choose the bins so that an equal number of g⁡(zi)g(z_{i}) in T2T_{2} land in each bin IjI_{j} for each j∈{1,…,B}j\in\{1,\dots,B\}—this uniform-mass binning scheme [10] as opposed to equal-width binning [9] is essential for being able to estimate the calibration error in Section 5.

Step 3 (Discretization): Discretize gg, by outputting the average gg value in each bin—these are the gray circles in Figure 1(c). Let μ⁡(S)=1|S|​∑s∈Ss\mu(S)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{s\in S}s denote the mean of a set of values SS. Let μ^​[j]=μ⁡({g⁡(zi)|g⁡(zi)∈Ij∧(zi,yi)∈T3})\hat{\mu}[j]=\mu(\{g(z_{i})\;|\;g(z_{i})\in I_{j}\wedge(z_{i},y_{i})\in T_{3}\}) be the mean of the g⁡(zi)g(z_{i}) values that landed in the jj-th bin. Recall that if z∈Ijz\in I_{j}, β⁡(z)=j\beta(z)=j is the interval z lands in. Then we set gℬ^​(z)=μ^​[β​(g​(z))]\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}}}(z)=\hat{\mu}[\beta(g(z))]—that is we simply output the mean value in the bin that g⁡(z)g(z) falls in.

4.2 Analysis

We now show that the scaling-binning calibrator requires O⁡(B+1/ϵ2)O(B+1/\epsilon^{2}) samples to calibrate, and in Section 5 we show that we can efficiently measure its calibration error. For the main theorem, we make some standard regularity assumptions on 𝒢\mathcal{G} which we formalize in Appendix D. Our result is a generalization result—we show that if 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains some g∗g^{*} with low calibration error, then our method is at least almost as well-calibrated as g∗g^{*} given sufficiently many samples.

Theorem 4.1 (Calibration bound).

Assume regularity conditions on 𝒢\mathcal{G} (finite parameters, injectivity, Lipschitz-continuity, consistency, twice differentiability). Given δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), there is a constant cc such that for all B,ϵ>0B,\epsilon>0, with n≥c⁡(B​log⁡B+log⁡Bϵ2)n\geq c\Big(B\log{B}+\frac{\log{B}}{\epsilon^{2}}\Big) samples, the scaling-binning calibrator finds g^ℬ\hat{g}_{\mathcal{B}} with (CE​(g^ℬ))2≤2​ming∈𝒢​(CE​(g))2+ϵ2(\textup{CE}(\hat{g}_{\mathcal{B}}))^{2}\leq 2\min_{g\in\mathcal{G}}(\textup{CE}(g))^{2}+\epsilon^{2}, with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta.

Note that our method can potentially be better calibrated than g∗g^{*}, because we bin the outputs of the scaling function, which reduces its calibration error (Proposition 3.3). While binning worsens the sharpness and can increase the mean-squared error of the model, in Proposition D.4 we show that if we use many bins, binning the outputs cannot increase the mean-squared error by much.

We prove Theorem 4.1 in Appendix D but give a sketch here. Step 1 of our algorithm is Platt scaling, which simply fits a function gg to the data—standard results in asymptotic statistics show that gg converges in O⁡(1ϵ2)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}) samples.

Step 3, where we bin the outputs of gg, is the main step of the algorithm. If we had infinite data, Proposition 3.3 showed that the binned version gℬg_{\mathcal{B}{}} has lower calibration error than gg, so we would be done. However we do not have infinite data—the core of our proof is to show that the empirically binned gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}} is within ϵ\epsilon of gℬg_{\mathcal{B}{}} in O⁡(B+1ϵ2)O(B+\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}) samples, instead of the O⁡(B+Bϵ2)O(B+\frac{B}{\epsilon^{2}}) samples required by histogram binning. The intuition is in Figure 1—the g⁡(zi)g(z_{i}) values in each bin (gray circles in Figure 1(c)) are in a narrower range than the yiy_{i} values (black crosses in Figure 1(b)) and thus have lower variance so when we take the average we incur less estimation error. The perhaps surprising part is that we are estimating BB numbers with O~​(1/ϵ2)\widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon^{2}) samples. In fact, there may be a small number of bins where the g⁡(zi)g(z_{i}) values are not in a narrow range, but our proof still shows that the overall estimation error is small.

Our uniform-mass binning scheme allows us to estimate the calibration error efficiently (see Section 5), unlike for scaling methods where we cannot estimate the calibration error (Section 3). Recall that we chose our bins so that each bin has an equal proportion of points in the recalibration set. Lemma 4.3 shows that this property approximately holds in the population as well. This allows us to estimate the calibration error efficiently (Theorem 5.4).

Definition 4.2 (Well-balanced binning).

Given a binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B} of size BB, and α≥1\alpha\geq 1. We say ℬ\mathcal{B} is α\alpha-well-balanced if for all jj,

1α​B≤ℙ⁡(Z∈Ij)≤αB\frac{1}{\alpha B}\leq\mathbb{P}(Z\in I_{j})\leq\frac{\alpha}{B}
Lemma 4.3.

For universal constant cc, if n≥c​B​log⁡Bδn\geq cB\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{} we chose is 2-well-balanced.

While the way we choose bins is not novel [10], we believe the guarantees around it are—not all binning schemes in the literature allow us to efficiently estimate the calibration error; for example, the binning scheme in [9] does not. Our proof of Lemma 4.3 is in Appendix D. We use a discretization argument to prove the result—this gives a tighter bound than applying Chernoff bounds or a standard VC dimension argument which would tell us we need O⁡(B2​log⁡Bδ)O(B^{2}\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}) samples.

4.3 Experiments

Our experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show that in the low-data regime, for example when we use ≤1000\leq 1000 data points to recalibrate, the scaling-binning calibrator produces models with much lower calibration error than histogram binning. The uncalibrated model outputs a confidence score associated with each class. We recalibrated each class separately as in [13], using BB bins per class, and evaluated calibration using the marginal calibration error (Definition 2.4).

We describe our experimental protocol for CIFAR-10. The CIFAR-10 validation set has 10,000 data points. We sampled, with replacement, a recalibration set of 1,000 points. We ran either the scaling-binning calibrator (we fit a sigmoid in the function fitting step) or histogram binning and measured the marginal calibration error on the entire set of 10K points. We repeated this entire procedure 100 times and computed mean and 90% confidence intervals, and we repeated this varying the number of bins BB. Figure 3(a) shows that the scaling-binning calibrator produces models with lower calibration error, for example 35%35\% lower calibration error when we use 100 bins per class.

Using more bins allows a model to produce more fine-grained predictions, e.g. [18] use B=51B=51 bins, which improves the quality of predictions as measured by the mean-squared error—Figure 3(b) shows that our method achieves better mean-squared errors for any given calibration constraint. More concretely, the figure shows a scatter plot of the mean-squared error and squared calibration error for histogram binning and the scaling-binning calibrator when we vary the number of bins. For example, if we want our models to have a calibration error ≤0.02=2%\leq 0.02=2\% we get a 9%9\% lower mean-squared error. In Appendix E we show that we get 5x lower top-label calibration error on ImageNet, and give further experiment details.

Validating theoretical bounds: In Appendix E we run synthetic experiments to validate the bound in Theorem 4.1. In particular, we show that if we fix the number of samples nn, and vary the number of bins BB, the squared calibration error for the scaling-binning calibrator is nearly constant but for histogram binning increases nearly linearly with BB. For both methods, the squared calibration error decreases approximately as 1/n1/n—that is when we double the number of samples the squared calibration error halves.

5 Verifying calibration

Before deploying our model we would like to check that it has calibration error below some desired threshold ℰ\mathcal{E}{}. In this section we show that we can accurately estimate the calibration error of binned models, if the binning scheme is 2-well-balanced. Recent work in machine learning uses a plugin estimate for each term in the calibration error [7, 15, 16, 17]. Older work in meteorology [18, 19] notices that this is a biased estimate, and proposes a debiased estimator that subtracts off an approximate correction term to reduce the bias. Our contribution is to show that the debiased estimator is more accurate: while the plugin estimator requires samples proportional to BB to estimate the calibration error, the debiased estimator requires samples proportional to B\sqrt{B}. Note that we show an improved sample complexity—prior work only showed that the naive estimator is biased. In Appendix G we also propose a way to debias the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error (ECE), and show that we can estimate the ECE more accurately on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

Suppose we wish to measure the squared calibration error ℰ2\mathcal{E}^{2}{} of a binned model f:𝒳→Sf:\mathcal{X}\to S where S⊆[0,1]S\subseteq[0,1] and |S|=B|S|=B. Suppose we get an evaluation set Tn={(x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)}T_{n}=\{(x_{1},y_{1}),\dots,(x_{n},y_{n})\}. Past work typically estimates the calibration error by directly estimating each term from samples:

Definition 5.1 (Plugin estimator).

Let LsL_{s} denote the yjy_{j} values where the model outputs ss: Ls={yj|(xj,yj)∈Tn∧f⁡(xj)=s}L_{s}=\{y_{j}\;|\;(x_{j},y_{j})\in T_{n}\wedge f(x_{j})=s\}. Let p^s\hat{p}_{s} be the estimated probability of ff outputting ss: p^s=|Ls|n\hat{p}_{s}=\frac{|L_{s}|}{n}.

Let y^s\hat{y}_{s} be the empirical average of YY when the model outputs ss: y^s=∑y∈Lsy|Ls|\hat{y}_{s}=\sum_{y\in L_{s}}\frac{y}{|L_{s}|}.

The plugin estimate for the squared calibration error is the weighted squared difference between y^s\hat{y}_{s} and ss:

ℰ^pl2=∑s∈Sp^s​(s−y^s)2\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}^{2}{}=\sum_{s\in S}\hat{p}_{s}(s-\hat{y}_{s})^{2}

Alternatively, [18, 19] propose to subtract an approximation of the bias from the estimate:

Definition 5.2 (Debiased estimator).

The debiased estimator for the squared calibration error is:

ℰ^db2=∑s∈Sp^s​[(s−y^s)2−y^s​(1−y^s)p^s​n−1]\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{db}}^{2}{}=\sum_{s\in S}\hat{p}_{s}\Big[(s-\hat{y}_{s})^{2}-\frac{\hat{y}_{s}(1-\hat{y}_{s})}{\hat{p}_{s}n-1}\Big]

We are interested in analyzing the number of samples required to estimate the calibration error within a constant multiplicative factor, that is to give an estimate ℰ^2\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{2}{} such that |ℰ^2−ℰ2|≤12​ℰ2\lvert\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{2}{}-\mathcal{E}^{2}{}\rvert\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}{} (where 12\frac{1}{2} can be replaced by any constant rr with 0<r<10<r<1). Our main result is that the plugin estimator requires O~​(Bℰ2)\widetilde{O}(\frac{B}{\mathcal{E}^{2}{}}) samples (Theorem 5.3) while the debiased estimator requires O~​(Bℰ2)\widetilde{O}(\frac{\sqrt{B}}{\mathcal{E}^{2}{}}) samples (Theorem 5.4).

Theorem 5.3 (Plugin estimator bound).

Suppose we have a binned model with squared calibration error ℰ2\mathcal{E}^{2}{}, where the binning scheme is 2-well-balanced, that is for all s∈Ss\in S, ℙ⁡(f⁡(X)=s)≥12​B\mathbb{P}(f(X)=s)\geq\frac{1}{2B}. 11 1 We do not need the upper bound of the 2-well-balanced property. If n≥c​Bℰ2​log⁡Bδn\geq c\frac{B}{\mathcal{E}^{2}{}}\log{\frac{B}{\delta}} for some universal constant cc, then for the plugin estimator, we have 12​ℰ2≤ℰ^pl2≤32​ℰ2\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}{}\leq\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}^{2}{}\leq\frac{3}{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}{} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Theorem 5.4 (Debiased estimator bound).

Suppose we have a binned model with squared calibration error ℰ2\mathcal{E}^{2}{} and for all s∈Ss\in S, ℙ⁡(f⁡(X)=s)≥12​B\mathbb{P}(f(X)=s)\geq\frac{1}{2B}. If n≥c​Bℰ2​log⁡Bδn\geq c\frac{\sqrt{B}}{\mathcal{E}^{2}{}}\log{\frac{B}{\delta}} for some universal constant cc then for the debiased estimator, we have 12​ℰ2≤ℰ^db2≤32​ℰ2\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}{}\leq\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{db}}^{2}{}\leq\frac{3}{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}{} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

The proofs of both theorems is in Appendix F. The idea is that for the plugin estimator, each term in the sum has bias 1/n1/n. These biases accumulate, giving total bias B/nB/n. The debiased estimator has much lower bias and the estimation variance cancels across bins—this intuition is captured in Lemma F.8 which requires careful conditioning to make the argument go through.

5.1 Experiments

We run a multiclass marginal calibration experiment on CIFAR-10 which suggests that the debiased estimator produces better estimates of the calibration error than the plugin estimator. We split the validation set of size 10,000 into two sets SCS_{C}{} and SES_{E}{} of sizes 3,000 and 7,000 respectively. We use SCS_{C}{} to re-calibrate and discretize a trained VGG-16 model. We calibrate each of the K=10K=10 classes seprately as described in Section 2 and used B=100B=100 or B=10B=10 bins per class. For varying values of nn, we sample nn points with replacement from SES_{E}{}, and estimate the calibration error using the debiased estimator and the plugin estimator. We then compute the squared deviation of these estimates from the squared calibration error measured on the entire set SES_{E}{}. We repeat this resampling 1,000 times to get the mean squared deviation of the estimates from the ground truth and confidence intervals. Figure 4(a) shows that the debiased estimates are much closer to the ground truth than the plugin estimates—the difference is especially significant when the number of samples nn is small or the number of bins BB is large. Note that having a perfect estimate corresponds to 00 on the vertical axis.

In Appendix G, we include histograms of the absolute difference between the estimates and ground truth for the plugin and debiased estimator, over the 1,000 resamples.

6 Related work

Calibration, including the squared calibration error, has been studied in many fields besides machine learning including meteorology [2, 3, 4, 5, 6], fairness [29, 30], healthcare [1, 31, 32, 33], reinforcement learning [34], natural language processing [7, 8], speech recognition [35], econometrics [25], and psychology [36]. Besides the calibration error, prior work also uses the Hosmer-Lemeshov test [37] and reliability diagrams [4, 38] to evaluate calibration. Concurrent work to ours [39] also notice that using the plugin calibration error estimator to test for calibration leads to rejecting well-calibrated models too often. Besides calibration, other ways of producing and quantifying uncertainties include Bayesian methods [40] and conformal prediction [41, 42].

Recalibration is related to (conditional) density estimation [44, 45] as the goal is to estimate 𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)]. Algorithms and analysis in density estimation typically assume the true density is L−L-Lipschitz, while in calibration applications, the calibration error of the final model should be measurable from data, without making untestable assumptions on LL.

Bias is a common issue with statistical estimators, for example, the seminal work by Stein [43] fixes the bias of the mean-squared error. However, debiasing an estimator does not typically lead to an improved sample complexity, as it does in our case.

7 Conclusion

This paper makes three contributions: 1. We showed that the calibration error of continuous methods is underestimated; 2. We introduced the first method, to our knowledge, that has better sample complexity than histogram binning and has a measurable calibration error, giving us the best of scaling and binning methods; and 3. We showed that an alternative estimator for calibration error has better sample complexity than the plugin estimator. There are many exciting avenues for future work:

  1. 1.

    Dataset shifts: Can we maintain calibration under dataset shifts? When the dataset shifts (for example, train on MNIST, but evaluate on SVHN) it is difficult to get very high accuracies on the target dataset, but can we at least know when our model is accurate and when it is not, or in other words can we ensure our model is calibrated on the new dataset? When a small amount of labeled target data is available, we can simply re-calibrate using the labeled target data since recalibration simply involves tuning a small number of parameters and therefore requires very few samples. However, can we maintain calibration when we do not have labeled examples from the target dataset?

  2. 2.

    Measuring calibration: Can we come up with alternative metrics that still capture a notion of calibration, but are measurable for scaling methods?

  3. 3.

    Multiclass calibration: Most papers on calibration focus on top-label calibration—can we come up with better methods for marginal calibration, so that each class prediction is calibrated? Can we achieve stronger notions of calibration, such as joint calibration, efficiently?

  4. 4.

    Better binning: Can we devise better ways of binning? While binning makes the calibration error measurable, it leads to an increase in the mean-squared error. In Proposition D.4 we bound the increase in MSE for the well-balanced binning scheme. However, in Section D.3 we give intuition for why other binning schemes may have a smaller increase in MSE.

  5. 5.

    Finite sample guarantees: Can we prove finite sample guarantees for Theorem 4.1 which show the dependency on the dimension and probability of failure?

  6. 6.

    Estimating calibration: The plugin estimator for the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error (called the ECE in [9, 24]) is also biased—can we come up with a more sample efficient estimator for the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error? In Appendix G we also propose a heuristic way to debias the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error and show strong experimental results, but can we prove guarantees for this? For the L2L^{2} calibration error, can we devise an even better estimator? If not, can we prove minimax lower bounds on this?

Appendix B Proofs for Section 3

The results in Section 3 hold more generally for ℓp​-CE\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}{} and not just CE. We recall the definition of ℓp​-CE\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}{}:

Definition B.1.

For p≥1p\geq 1, the ℓp\ell_{p} calibration error of f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] is given by:

ℓp​-CE​(f)=(𝔼[|f⁡(X)−𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)]|p])1/p\displaystyle\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f)=\Big(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\big[\left|f(X)-\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)]\right|^{p}\big]\Big)^{1/p} (5)

We now restate and prove the results in terms of ℓp​-CE\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}{} which implies the result for CE in the paper as a special case, but also for other commonly used metrics such as the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error (ECE).

Restatement of Example 3.2.

For any binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{}, p≥1p\geq 1, and continuous bijective function f:[0,1]→[0,1]f:[0,1]\to[0,1], there exists a distribution PP over 𝒳,𝒴\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} s.t. ℓp​-CE​(fℬ)=0\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}})=0 but ℓp​-CE​(f)≥0.49\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f)\geq 0.49. Note that for all ff, 0≤ℓp​-CE​(f)≤10\leq\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f)\leq 1.

Proof.

As stated in the main text, the intuition is that in each interval IjI_{j} in ℬ\mathcal{B}{}, the model could underestimate the true probability 𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)] half the time, and overestimate the probability half the time. So if we average over the entire bin the model appears to be calibrated, even though it is very uncalibrated. The proof simply formalizes this intuition.

Since ff is bijective and continuous we can select data distribution PP s.t. f⁡(X)∼Uniform​[0.5−ϵ,0.5+ϵ]f(X)\sim\mbox{Uniform}[0.5-\epsilon,0.5+\epsilon] for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0. To see this, first note that from real analysis since f:[0,1]→[0,1]f:[0,1]\to[0,1] and ff is bijective and continuous, f−1f^{-1} is also bijective and continuous. Then we can let X∼f−1​(Uniform​[0.5−ϵ,0.5+ϵ])X\sim f^{-1}(\mbox{Uniform}[0.5-\epsilon,0.5+\epsilon]) which has the desired property and has a density.

Now, consider each interval IjI_{j} in binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{}, and let Aj=Ij∩Uniform​[0.5−ϵ,0.5+ϵ]A_{j}=I_{j}\cap\mbox{Uniform}[0.5-\epsilon,0.5+\epsilon]. Note that 𝔼[f⁡(X)∣f⁡(X)∈Aj]=𝔼[f⁡(X)∣f⁡(X)∈Ij]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[f(X)\mid f(X)\in A_{j}]=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[f(X)\mid f(X)\in I_{j}]. Since f⁡(X)∈[0.5−ϵ,0.5+ϵ]f(X)\in[0.5-\epsilon,0.5+\epsilon], pj∈[0.5−ϵ,0.5+ϵ]p_{j}\in[0.5-\epsilon,0.5+\epsilon] as well. We will choose P⁡(Y)P(Y) so that YY is 11 whenever f⁡(X)f(X) lands in the first pjp_{j} fraction of interval AjA_{j}, and 00 whenever f⁡(X)f(X) lands in the latter 1−pj1-p_{j} fraction of AjA_{j}. Then 𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)∈Aj]=pj\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)\in A_{j}]=p_{j}, so the binned calibration error is 0. But notice that for all s∈[0.5−ϵ,0.5+ϵ]s\in[0.5-\epsilon,0.5+\epsilon], 𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)=s]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)=s] is either 00 or 11. So we have:

|𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)=s]−s|≥0.5−ϵ\lvert\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)=s]-s\rvert\geq 0.5-\epsilon

That is, at every point the model is actually very miscalibrated at each ss. By taking ϵ\epsilon very small, we then get that ℓp​-CE​(p)≥0.5−ϵ′\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(p)\geq 0.5-\epsilon^{\prime} for any ϵ′>0\epsilon^{\prime}>0, which completes the proof. ∎

Restatement of Proposition 3.3.

Given any binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{} and model f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1], we have:

ℓp​-CE​(fℬ)≤ℓp​-CE​(f).\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}})\leq\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f).
Proof.

It suffices to prove the claim for the ℓpp\ell_{p}^{p} error:

(ℓp​-CE​(fℬ))p≤(ℓp​-CE​(f))p(\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}}))^{p}\leq(\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f))^{p}

This is because if p>0p>0 then a≤b⇔ap≤bpa\leq b\Leftrightarrow a^{p}\leq b^{p}.

For p≥1p\geq 1, let l⁡(a,b)=(|a−b|)pl(a,b)=(|a-b|)^{p}. We note that ll is convex in both arguments. The proof is now a simple result of Jensen’s inequality and convexity of ll. Suppose that ℬ\mathcal{B} is given by intervals I1,…,IBI_{1},...,I_{B}. Let Z=f⁡(X)Z=f(X)—note that ZZ is a random variable.

We can write (ℓp​-CE​(fℬ))p(\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}}))^{p} as:

(ℓp​-CE​(fℬ))p=∑j=1BP⁡(Z∈Ij)​l​(𝔼⁡[Z∣Z∈Ij],𝔼⁡[Y∣Z∈Ij])(\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}}))^{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{B}P(Z\in I_{j})\;l\Big(\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Z\in I_{j}],\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z\in I_{j}]\Big)

We can write (ℓp​-CE​(f))p(\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f))^{p} as:

(ℓp​-CE​(f))p=∑j=1BP⁡(Z∈Ij)​𝔼​[l⁡(Z,𝔼⁡[Y∣Z])∣Z∈Ij](\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f))^{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{B}P(Z\in I_{j})\;\mathbb{E}\Big[l\big(Z,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z]\big)\mid Z\in I_{j}\Big]

Fix some bin Ij∈ℬI_{j}\in\mathcal{B}{}. By Jensen’s inequality,

l⁡(𝔼⁡[Z∣Z∈Ij],𝔼⁡[Y∣Z∈Ij])≤𝔼⁡[l⁡(Z,𝔼⁡[Y∣Z])∣Z∈Ij]l\Big(\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Z\in I_{j}],\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z\in I_{j}]\Big)\leq\mathbb{E}\Big[l\big(Z,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z]\big)\mid Z\in I_{j}\Big]

Since this inequality holds for each term in the sum, it holds for the whole sum:

(ℓp​-CE​(fℬ))p≤(ℓp​-CE​(f))p(\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}}))^{p}\leq(\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f))^{p}

Note that the proof also implies that finer binning schemes give a better lower bound. That is, given ℬ′\mathcal{B}{}^{\prime} suppose for all Ij′∈ℬ′I_{j}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}{}^{\prime}, Ij′⊆IkI_{j}^{\prime}\subseteq I_{k} for some Ik∈ℬI_{k}\in\mathcal{B}{}. Then ℓp-CE(fℬ)≤ℓp-CE(fℬ′)≤ℓp-CE(f)\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}})\leq\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}^{\prime}})\leq\ell_{p}\textup{-CE}(f). This is because fℬ′f_{\mathcal{B}{}^{\prime}} can be seen as a binned version of fℬf_{\mathcal{B}{}}.

∎

Appendix C Ablations for Section 3

Here we present additional experiments for Section 3. Recall that the experiments in section 3 showed that binning underestimates the calibration error of a model—we focused on the ℓ2​-CE\ell_{2}\mbox{-CE} and selected bins so that each bin has an equal number of data points. Figure 5(a) shows that binning is also unreliable at measuring the ℓ1​-CE\ell_{1}\mbox{-CE} (ECE) on ImageNet—using more bins uncovers a higher calibration error than we would otherwise detect with fewer bins. Figure 5(b) shows that the same conclusion holds on ImageNet if we look at the ℓ1​-CE\ell_{1}\mbox{-CE} and use an alternative approach to selecting bins used in [9] that we call equal-width binning. Here, the BB bins are selected to be I1=[0,1B],I2=(1B,2B],…,IB=(B−1B,1]I_{1}=[0,\frac{1}{B}],I_{2}=(\frac{1}{B},\frac{2}{B}],\dots,I_{B}=(\frac{B-1}{B},1]. The experimental protocol is the same as in section 3.

We repeated both of these experiments on CIFAR-10 as well, and plot the results in Figure 6. Here the results are inconclusive because the error bars are large. This is because the CIFAR-10 dataset is smaller than ImageNet, and the accuracy of the CIFAR-10 model is 93.1%, so the calibration error that we are trying to measure is much smaller.

We provide details on the dataset split for CIFAR-10. For CIFAR-10, we used a VGG16 model and split the test set into 3 sets of size (1000,1000,8000)(1000,1000,8000), where used the first set of data to recalibrate the model using Platt scaling, the second to select the binning scheme, and the third to measure the binned calibration error. As stated in the main body of the paper, for ImageNet we used a split of (20000,5000,25000)(20000,5000,25000).

Appendix D Proofs for section 4

Our analysis of the sample complexity of the scaling-binning calibrator requires some assumptions on the function family 𝒢\mathcal{G}{}:

  1. 1.

    (Finite parameters). Let 𝒢={gθ:[0,1]→[0,1]|θ∈A}\mathcal{G}{}=\{g_{\theta}:[0,1]\to[0,1]\;|\;\theta\in A\} where A⊆ℝdA\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and AA is open.

  2. 2.

    (Injective). For all gθ∈𝒢g_{\theta}\in\mathcal{G}{} we assume gθg_{\theta} is injective.

  3. 3.

    (Consistency). Intuitively, consistency means that given infinite data, the estimated parameters should converge to the unique optimal parameters in AA. More formally, suppose θ∗=arg​minθ∈A⁡MSE​(gθ)\theta^{*}=\argmin_{\theta\in A}\textup{MSE}(g_{\theta}). Then the parameters θ^n\hat{\theta}_{n} estimated by minimizing the empirical MSE with nn samples in step 1 of the algorithm, converges in distribution to θ∗\theta^{*}, that is, θ^n→Dθ∗\hat{\theta}_{n}\to_{D}\theta^{*} as n→∞n\to\infty. Note that consistency inherently assumes identifiability, that there is a unique minimizer θ∗\theta^{*} in the open set AA.

  4. 4.

    (Regularity). We assume that regularity conditions in Theorem 5.23 of [50] hold, which require the loss to be twice differentiable with symmetric, non-singular Hessian, and that gθ​(x)g_{\theta}(x) is Lipschitz in θ\theta for all xx. We will also require the second derivative to be continuous.

We assume that 𝒢\mathcal{G}{} satisfies these assumptions in the rest of this section. Note that aside from injectivity, the remaining conditions are only required for the (fairly standard) analysis of step 1 of the algorithm, which says that a parametric scaling method with a small number of parameters will quickly converge to its optimal error.

D.1 Calibration bound (Proof of Theorem 4.1)

The goal is to prove the following theorem from Section 4, which we restate:

Restatement of Theorem 4.1.

Assume regularity conditions on 𝒢\mathcal{G} (finite parameters, injectivity, Lipschitz-continuity, consistency, twice differentiability). Given δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), there is a constant cc such that for all B,ϵ>0B,\epsilon>0, with n≥c⁡(B​log⁡B+log⁡Bϵ2)n\geq c\Big(B\log{B}+\frac{\log{B}}{\epsilon^{2}}\Big) samples, the scaling-binning calibrator finds g^ℬ\hat{g}_{\mathcal{B}} with (CE​(g^ℬ))2≤2​ming∈𝒢​(CE​(g))2+ϵ2(\textup{CE}(\hat{g}_{\mathcal{B}}))^{2}\leq 2\min_{g\in\mathcal{G}}(\textup{CE}(g))^{2}+\epsilon^{2}, with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta.

We will analyze each step of our algorithm and then combine the pieces to get Theorem 4.1. As we mention in the main text, step 3 is the main step, so Lemma D.2 is one of the core parts of our proof. Step 2 is where we construct a binning scheme so that each bin has an equal number of points—we show that this property holds approximately in the population (Lemma 4.3). This is important as well, particularly to ensure we can estimate the calibration error. Step 1 is basically Platt scaling, and the asymptotic analysis is fairly standard.

Step 3: Our proofs will require showing convergence in ℓ2\ell_{2} and ℓ1\ell_{1} norm in function space, which we define below:

Definition D.1 (Distances between functions).

Given f,g:[0,1]→[0,1]f,g:[0,1]\to[0,1], for the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm we define ‖f−g‖22=𝔼[(f⁡(Z)−g⁡(Z))2]||f-g||_{2}^{2}=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(f(Z)-g(Z))^{2}] and ‖f−g‖2=‖f−g‖22||f-g||_{2}=\sqrt{||f-g||_{2}^{2}}. For the ℓ1\ell_{1} norm we define ‖f−g‖1=𝔼[|f⁡(Z)−g⁡(Z)|]||f-g||_{1}=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\lvert f(Z)-g(Z)\rvert]

Recall that we showed that in the limit of infinite data the binned version of gg, gℬg_{\mathcal{B}{}}, has lower calibration error than gg (Proposition 3.3). However our method uses nn data points to empirically bin gg, giving us gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}. We now show the key lemma that allows us to bound the calibration error and later the mean-squared error. That is, we show that the empirically binned function gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}} quickly converges to gℬg_{\mathcal{B}{}} in both ℓ2\ell_{2} and ℓ1\ell_{1} norms.

Lemma D.2 (Empirical binning).

There exist constants cB,c1,c2c_{B},c_{1},c_{2} such that the following is true. Given g:[0,1]→[0,1]g:[0,1]\to[0,1], binning set T3={(zi,yi)}i=1nT_{3}=\{(z_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} and a 2-well-balanced binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{} of size BB. Given 0<δ<0.50<\delta<0.5, suppose that n≥cB​B​log⁡Bδn\geq c_{B}B\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}. Then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, ‖gℬ^−gℬ‖2≤c2n​log⁡Bδ||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-g_{\mathcal{B}{}}||_{2}\leq\frac{c_{2}}{\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}} and ‖gℬ^−gℬ‖1≤c1n​B​log⁡Bδ||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-g_{\mathcal{B}{}}||_{1}\leq\frac{c_{1}}{\sqrt{nB}}\sqrt{\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}}

Step 2: Recall that we chose our bins so that each bin had an equal proportion of points in the recalibration set. In our proofs we required that this property (approximately) holds in the population as well. The following lemma shows this.

Restatement of Lemma 4.3.

For universal constant cc, if n≥c​B​log⁡Bδn\geq cB\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{} we chose is 2-well-balanced.

Proof.

Suppose we are given a bin construction set of size nn, Tn={(z1,y1),…,(zn,yn)}T_{n}=\{(z_{1},y_{1}),\dots,(z_{n},y_{n})\}. For any interval II, let P^​(I)\hat{P}(I) be the empirical estimate of P⁡(I)=ℙ⁡(g⁡(Z)∈I)P(I)=\mathbb{P}(g(Z)\in I) given by:

P^​(I)=|{(zi,yi)∈Tn∣g⁡(zi)∈I}|n\hat{P}(I)=\frac{|\{(z_{i},y_{i})\in T_{n}\mid g(z_{i})\in I\}|}{n}

We constructed the bins so that each interval IjI_{j} contains nB\frac{n}{B} points, or in other words, P^​(Ij)=1B\hat{P}(I_{j})=\frac{1}{B}. We want to show that 12​B≤ℙ⁡(g⁡(Z)∈Ij)≤2B\frac{1}{2B}\leq\mathbb{P}(g(Z)\in I_{j})\leq\frac{2}{B}. Since the intervals are chosen from data, we want a uniform concentration result that holds for all such intervals IjI_{j}.

We will use a discretization argument. The idea is that we will cover [0,1][0,1] with 10​B10B disjoint small intervals such that for each of these intervals Ij′I_{j}^{\prime}, P⁡(g⁡(Z)∈Ij′)=110​BP(g(Z)\in I_{j}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{10B}. Given an arbitrary interval II, we can write it as an approximate union of these small intervals, which will allow us to concentrate |P​(I)−P^​(I)||P(I)-\hat{P}(I)|.

Concentrating the small intervals: Fix some interval Ij′I_{j}^{\prime}. Let wi=𝕀⁡(g⁡(zi)∈Ij′)w_{i}=\mathbb{I}(g(z_{i})\in I_{j}^{\prime}) for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. Then wi∼Bernoulli​(110​B)w_{i}\sim\mbox{Bernoulli}(\frac{1}{10B}). P^​(Ij′)\hat{P}(I_{j}^{\prime}) is simply the empirical average of nn such values and as such with probability at least 1−δ10​B1-\frac{\delta}{10B}:

|P⁡(Ij′)−Pj^​(Ij′)|≤210​B​n​log⁡10​Bδ+23​n​log⁡10​Bδ|P(I_{j}^{\prime})-\hat{P_{j}}(I_{j}^{\prime})|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2}{10Bn}\log{\frac{10B}{\delta}}}+\frac{2}{3n}\log{\frac{10B}{\delta}}
