|P⁡(Ij′)−Pj^​(Ij′)|≤1100​B|P(I_{j}^{\prime})-\hat{P_{j}}(I_{j}^{\prime})|\leq\frac{1}{100B}

And this was with probability at least 1−δ10​B1-\frac{\delta}{10B}. So by union bound we get that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta this holds for all Ij′I_{j}^{\prime}.

Concentrating arbitrary intervals: Now consider arbitrary I⊆[0,1]I\subseteq[0,1]. We can approximately write II as a union of the small Ij′I_{j}^{\prime} intervals. More concretely, we can form a lower bound for P^​(I)\hat{P}(I) by considering all Ij′I_{j}^{\prime} contained in II:

SL={Ij′∣Ij′⊆I}S_{L}=\{I_{j}^{\prime}\mid I_{j}^{\prime}\subseteq I\}

Similarly we can form an upper bound for P^​(I)\hat{P}(I) by considering all Ij′I_{j}^{\prime} that have non-empty intersection with II:

SU={Ij′∣Ij′∩I≠∅}S_{U}=\{I_{j}^{\prime}\mid I_{j}^{\prime}\cap I\neq\emptyset\}

We can then show:

910​P​(I)−15​B≤P^​(I)≤1110​P​(I)+15​B\frac{9}{10}P(I)-\frac{1}{5B}\leq\hat{P}(I)\leq\frac{11}{10}P(I)+\frac{1}{5B}

Since in our case for all jj, P^​(Ij)=1B\hat{P}(I_{j})=\frac{1}{B}, this gives us:

12​B≤P⁡(Ij)≤2B\frac{1}{2B}\leq P(I_{j})\leq\frac{2}{B}

∎

Step 1: Recall that step 1 essentially applies a scaling method—we fit a small number of parameters to the recalibration data. We show that if 𝒢\mathcal{G}{} contains g∗∈𝒢g^{*}\in\mathcal{G}{} with low calibration error, then the empirical risk minimizer g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}{} of the mean-squared loss will also quickly converge to low calibration error. Intuitively, methods like Platt scaling fit a single parameter to the data so standard results in asymptotic statistics tell us they will converge quickly to their optimal error, at least in mean-squared error. We can combine this with a decomposition of the mean-squared error into calibration and refinement, and the injectivity of g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}, to show they also converge quickly in calibration error.

Lemma D.3 (Convergence of scaling).

Given δ\delta, there exists a constant cc, such that for all nn, (CE​(g))2≤ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))2+cn(\textup{CE}(g))^{2}\leq\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+\frac{c}{n}, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Proof.

From calibration error to mean-squared error: We use the classic decomposition of the mean-squared error into calibration error (also known as reliability) and refinement22 2 Note that the refinement term can be further decomposed into resolution (also known as sharpness) and irreducible uncertainty.. For any g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}{} we have:

MSE​(g)=(CE​(g))2⏟calibration+𝔼[(𝔼[Y∣g⁡(Z)]−Y)2]⏟refinement\textup{MSE}(g)=\underbrace{(\textup{CE}(g))^{2}}_{\mbox{calibration}}+\underbrace{\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid g(Z)]-Y)^{2}]}_{\mbox{refinement}}

Note that the refinement term is constant for all injective g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}{}, since for injective gg:

𝔼[(𝔼[Y∣g⁡(Z)]−Y)2]=𝔼[(𝔼[Y∣Z]−Y)2]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid g(Z)]-Y)^{2}]=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid Z]-Y)^{2}]

This means that the difference in calibration error between any gg and g′g^{\prime} is precisely the difference in the mean-squared error. So it suffices to upper bound the generalization gap MSE​(g)−MSE​(g∗)\textup{MSE}(g)-\textup{MSE}(g^{*}) for the mean-squared error. Our analysis is fairly standard: we will show asymptotic convergence in the parameter space, and then use a Taylor expansion to show convergence in the MSE loss.

Parameter convergence: Recall that θ^\hat{\theta} denotes the parameters estimated by optimizing the empirical mean-squared error objective on nn samples in step 1 of our algorithm, and θ∗\theta^{*} denotes the optimal parameters that minimize the mean-squared error objective on the population. From Theorem 5.23 of [50], on the asymptotic parameter convergence of M-estimators, we have as n→∞n\to\infty:

n(θ^−θ∗)→DN(0,Σ)\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*})\to_{D}N(0,\Sigma)

Then for each 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d, we have:

n(θ^i−θi∗)→DN(0,σi2)\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i})\to_{D}N(0,\sigma_{i}^{2})

We will show that there exists cic_{i} such that for each ii and for all nn, with probability at least 1−δd1-\frac{\delta}{d}:

|θ^i−θi∗|≤cin\lvert\hat{\theta}_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i}\rvert\leq\frac{c_{i}}{n}

To see this, we begin with the definition of convergence in distribution, which says that the CDFs converge pointwise at every point where the CDF is continuous, which for a Gaussian is every point. That is, letting ziz_{i} be a sample from N⁡(0,σi2)N(0,\sigma_{i}^{2}), we have for all cc:

limn→∞ℙ⁡(n​(θ^i−θi∗)≥c)=ℙ⁡(zi≥c)\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i})\geq c)=\mathbb{P}(z_{i}\geq c)

By considering the CDF at each point and its negative, we can show the same result for the absolute value:

limn→∞ℙ⁡(n​|θ^i−θi∗|≥c)=ℙ⁡(|zi|≥c)\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{n}\lvert\hat{\theta}_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i}\rvert\geq c)=\mathbb{P}(\lvert z_{i}\rvert\geq c)

The tails of a normal distribution are bounded, so we can choose ci′c_{i}^{\prime} such that:

ℙ⁡(|zi|≥ci′)≤δ2​d\mathbb{P}(\lvert z_{i}\rvert\geq c_{i}^{\prime})\leq\frac{\delta}{2d}

By definition of limit, this means that we can choose NiN_{i} such that for all n≥Nin\geq N_{i}, we have:

ℙ⁡(n​|θ^i−θi∗|≥ci′)≤δd\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{n}\lvert\hat{\theta}_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i}\rvert\geq c_{i}^{\prime})\leq\frac{\delta}{d}

In other words, for all n≥Nin\geq N_{i}, with probability at least 1−δd1-\frac{\delta}{d}:

|θ^i−θi∗|≤ci′n\lvert\hat{\theta}_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i}\rvert\leq\frac{c_{i}^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}

Since this only does not hold for finitely many values 1,⋯,Ni−11,\cdots,N_{i}-1, we can ‘absorb’ these cases into the constant. That is, for each n∈{1,⋯,Ni−1}n\in\{1,\cdots,N_{i}-1\}, there exists rnr_{n} such that if we use nn samples, then except with probability δd\frac{\delta}{d}, |θ^i−θi∗|≤rn\lvert\hat{\theta}_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i}\rvert\leq r_{n}. So then we can choose cic_{i} such that for all nn:

|θ^i−θi∗|≤ci′+max1≤m<Ni⁡rm​mn≤cin\lvert\hat{\theta}_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i}\rvert\leq\frac{c_{i}^{\prime}+\max_{1\leq m<N_{i}}{r_{m}\sqrt{m}}}{\sqrt{n}}\leq\frac{c_{i}}{\sqrt{n}}

We apply union bound over the indices ii, and can then bound the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm of the difference between the estimated and optimal parameters, so that we can choose kk such that for all nn, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta:

‖θ^−θ∗‖22≤kn||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{k}{n}

Loss convergence: We denote the loss by LL, defined as:

L⁡(θ)=MSE​(gθ)=𝔼[(Y−gθ​(X))2]L(\theta)=\textup{MSE}(g_{\theta})=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(Y-g_{\theta}(X))^{2}]

We approximate the loss LL by the first few terms of its Taylor expansion, which we denote by L~\widetilde{L}:

L~(θ)=L(θ∗)+∇L(θ∗)T(θ^−θ∗)+(θ^−θ∗)T∇2L(θ∗)(θ^−θ∗)\widetilde{L}(\theta)=L(\theta^{*})+\nabla L(\theta^{*})^{T}(\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*})+(\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*})^{T}\nabla^{2}L(\theta^{*})(\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*})

We assumed that LL was twice differentiable with continuous second derivative, and that θ∗\theta^{*} minimized the loss in an open set, so ∇L​(θ∗)=0\nabla L(\theta^{*})=0, and we also have (see e.g. Theorem 3.3.18 in [51]):

lim‖θ^−θ∗‖2→0L​(θ^)−L~​(θ^)‖θ^−θ∗‖22=0\lim_{||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}\to 0}\frac{L(\hat{\theta})-\widetilde{L}(\hat{\theta})}{||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}^{2}}=0

By the definition of a limit if we fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists R>0R>0 such that if ‖θ^−θ∗‖2≤R||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}\leq R then L⁡(θ^)−L~​(θ^)≤ϵ​‖θ^−θ∗‖22L(\hat{\theta})-\widetilde{L}(\hat{\theta})\leq\epsilon||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}^{2}. For some large enough N0N_{0}, if n≥N0n\geq N_{0}, then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, ‖θ^−θ∗‖2≤R||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}\leq R. As before, since this only does not hold for finitely many NN, we can fold these cases into the constant so that there exists ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime} such that for all nn, L⁡(θ^)−L~​(θ^)≤ϵ′​‖θ^−θ∗‖22L(\hat{\theta})-\widetilde{L}(\hat{\theta})\leq\epsilon^{\prime}||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}^{2} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. Plugging in L~​(θ^)\widetilde{L}(\hat{\theta}), we have:

L⁡(θ^)−L⁡(θ∗)≤(θ^−θ∗)T​∇2L​(θ∗)​(θ^−θ∗)+ϵ′​‖θ^−θ∗‖22L(\hat{\theta})-L(\theta^{*})\leq(\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*})^{T}\nabla^{2}L(\theta^{*})(\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*})+\epsilon^{\prime}||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}^{2}

We can bound this by the operator norm of the Hessian, and then use the parameter convergence result:

L⁡(θ^)−L⁡(θ∗)≤(‖∇2L​(θ∗)‖o​p+ϵ′)​‖θ^−θ∗‖22≤cnL(\hat{\theta})-L(\theta^{*})\leq(||\nabla^{2}L(\theta^{*})||_{op}+\epsilon^{\prime})||\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}||_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{c}{n}

which holds with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, as desired.

∎

Finally, we have the tools to prove the main theorem:

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

The proof pieces together Lemmas D.3, D.2, 4.3 and Proposition 3.3.

For any fixed c1>0c_{1}>0, there exists c1′c_{1}^{\prime} such that if n≥c1′​(1ϵ2)n\geq c_{1}^{\prime}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}\big), from Lemma D.3, step 1 of our algorithm gives us gg with (CE​(g))2≤ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))2+c1​ϵ2(\textup{CE}(g))^{2}\leq\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+c_{1}\epsilon^{2}, with probability at least 1−δ31-\frac{\delta}{3}.

Next, for universal constant c2c_{2}, if n≥c2​(B​log⁡Bδ)n\geq c_{2}(B\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}), from Lemma 4.3, step 2 chooses a 2-well-balanced binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{} with probability at least 1−δ31-\frac{\delta}{3}.

From Proposition 3.3, (CE​(gℬ))2≤(CE​(g))2≤ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))2+c1​ϵ2(\textup{CE}(g_{\mathcal{B}{}}))^{2}\leq(\textup{CE}(g))^{2}\leq\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+c_{1}\epsilon^{2}. Then from Lemma D.2, for any c3>0c_{3}>0, there exists c3′c_{3}^{\prime} such that if n≥c3′​(1ϵ2​log⁡Bδ)n\geq c_{3}^{\prime}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}\big), step 3 gives us gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}} with ‖gℬ^−gℬ‖2≤c3​ϵ||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-g_{\mathcal{B}{}}||_{2}\leq c_{3}\epsilon with probability at least 1−δ31-\frac{\delta}{3}. We want to say that since gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}} is close to gℬg_{\mathcal{B}{}} and gℬg_{\mathcal{B}{}} has low calibration error, this must mean that gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}} has low calibration error.

To do this we represent the (ℓ2\ell_{2}) calibration error of any gg as the distance between gg and a perfectly recalibrated version of gg. That is, we define the perfectly recalibrated version of gg as:

ω⁡(g)​(z)=𝔼[Y∣g⁡(Z)=z]\omega(g)(z)=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid g(Z)=z]

Then for any gg, we can write CE​(g)=‖g−ω⁡(g)‖2\textup{CE}(g)=||g-\omega(g)||_{2}. By triangle inequality on the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm on functions, we have:

‖gℬ^−ω⁡(gℬ)‖2≤||gℬ^−gℬ||2+‖gℬ−ω⁡(gℬ)‖2≤c3​ϵ+ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))2+c1​ϵ2||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-\omega(g_{\mathcal{B}{}})||_{2}\leq||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-g_{\mathcal{B}{}}||_{2}+||g_{\mathcal{B}{}}-\omega(g_{\mathcal{B}{}})||_{2}\leq c_{3}\epsilon+\sqrt{\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+c_{1}\epsilon^{2}}

Now the LHS is not quite the calibration error of gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}, which is ‖gℬ^−ω⁡(gℬ^)‖2||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-\omega(\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}})||_{2} 33 3 This is a very technical point, so at a first pass the reader may skip the following discussion.. However, since gg is injective, gℬg_{\mathcal{B}{}} takes on a different value for each interval Ij∈ℬI_{j}\in\mathcal{B}{}. If gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}} also takes on a different value for each interval Ij∈ℬI_{j}\in\mathcal{B}{}, then we can see that ω⁡(gℬ)=ω⁡(gℬ^)\omega(g_{\mathcal{B}{}})=\omega(\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}). If not, ω⁡(gℬ^)\omega(\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}) can only merge some of the intervals of ω⁡(gℬ)\omega(g_{\mathcal{B}{}}), and by Jensen’s we can show:

‖gℬ^−ω⁡(gℬ^)‖2≤‖gℬ^−ω⁡(gℬ)‖2≤c3​ϵ+ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))2+c1​ϵ2||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-\omega(\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}})||_{2}\leq||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-\omega(g_{\mathcal{B}{}})||_{2}\leq c_{3}\epsilon+\sqrt{\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+c_{1}\epsilon^{2}}

An alternative way to see this is to add infinitesimal noise to gℬ^\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}} for each interval IjI_{j}, in which case we get ω⁡(gℬ)=ω⁡(gℬ^)\omega(g_{\mathcal{B}{}})=\omega(\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}). Finally we convert back from CE to the squared calibration error:

(CE​(gℬ^))2=‖gℬ^−ω⁡(gℬ^)‖22≤ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))2+(c32+c1)​ϵ2+2​(c32​ϵ2)​(ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))2+c1​ϵ2)(\textup{CE}(\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}))^{2}=||\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}-\omega(\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}})||_{2}^{2}\leq\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+(c_{3}^{2}+c_{1})\epsilon^{2}+2\sqrt{(c_{3}^{2}\epsilon^{2})\big(\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+c_{1}\epsilon^{2}\big)}

By the AM-GM inequality, we have:

2​(c32​ϵ2)​(ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))2+c1​ϵ2)≤(c32+c1)​ϵ2+ming′∈𝒢⁡(CE​(g′))22\sqrt{(c_{3}^{2}\epsilon^{2})\big(\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+c_{1}\epsilon^{2}\big)}\leq(c_{3}^{2}+c_{1})\epsilon^{2}+\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}

Combining these, we get:

(CE​(gℬ^))2≤2​ming′∈𝒢​(CE​(g′))2+2​(c32+c1)​ϵ2(\textup{CE}(\hat{g_{\mathcal{B}{}}}))^{2}\leq 2\min_{g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}{}}(\textup{CE}(g^{\prime}))^{2}+2(c_{3}^{2}+c_{1})\epsilon^{2}

By e.g. choosing c1=0.1c_{1}=0.1 and c3=0.1c_{3}=0.1, we have 2​(c32+c1)≤12(c_{3}^{2}+c_{1})\leq 1, which gives us the desired result. By union bound over each step, we have this with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

∎

D.2 Bounding the mean-squared error

We also show that if we use lots of bins, discretization has little impact on model quality as measured by the mean-squared error. Note that recalibration itself typically reduces/improves the mean-squared error. However, in our method after fitting a recalibration function like Platt scaling does, we discretize the function outputs. This reduces the calibration error and allows us to measure the calibration error, but it does increase the mean-squared error by a small amount. Here we upper bound the increase in mean-squared error. In other words, our method allows for the calibration error of the final model to be measured, and has little impact on the mean-squared error.

Proposition D.4 (MSE Bound).

If ℬ\mathcal{B} is a 2-well-balanced binning scheme of size BB and B=Ω~​(n)B=\widetilde{\Omega}(n), where Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} hides log\log factors, then MSE​(g^ℬ)≤MSE​(g)+O⁡(1B)\textup{MSE}(\hat{g}_{\mathcal{B}})\leq\textup{MSE}(g)+O(\frac{1}{B}).

To show this we begin with a lemma showing that if ff and gg are close in ℓ1\ell_{1} norm, then their mean-squared errors are close:

Lemma D.5.

For f,g:[0,1]→[0,1]f,g:[0,1]\to[0,1], MSE​(f)≤MSE​(g)+2​‖f−g‖1\textup{MSE}(f)\leq\textup{MSE}(g)+2||f-g||_{1}.

Proof.
𝔼[(f⁡(Z)−Y)2−(g⁡(Z)−Y)2]\displaystyle\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(f(Z)-Y)^{2}-(g(Z)-Y)^{2}] =𝔼[(f⁡(Z)−g⁡(Z))​(f⁡(Z)+g⁡(Z)−2​Y)]\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(f(Z)-g(Z))(f(Z)+g(Z)-2Y)]
≤𝔼[|f⁡(Z)−g⁡(Z)|​|f⁡(Z)+g⁡(Z)−2​Y|]\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[|f(Z)-g(Z)||f(Z)+g(Z)-2Y|]
≤𝔼[2​|f⁡(Z)−g⁡(Z)|]\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[2|f(Z)-g(Z)|]
=2​‖f−g‖1\displaystyle=2||f-g||_{1}

Where the third line followed because −2≤f⁡(Z)+g⁡(Z)−2​Y≤2-2\leq f(Z)+g(Z)-2Y\leq 2. ∎

Next, we show that in the limit of infinite data, if we bin with a well-balanced binning scheme then the MSE cannot increase by much.

Lemma D.6.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be an α\alpha-well-balanced binning scheme of size BB. Then MSE​(gℬ)≤MSE​(g)+2​αB\textup{MSE}(g_{\mathcal{B}})\leq\textup{MSE}(g)+\frac{2\alpha}{B}.

Proof.

We bound ‖gℬ−g‖1||g_{\mathcal{B}}-g||_{1} and then use Lemma D.5. We use the law of total expectation, conditioning on β⁡(g⁡(Z))\beta(g(Z)), the bin that g⁡(Z)g(Z) falls into.

‖gℬ−g‖1\displaystyle||g_{\mathcal{B}}-g||_{1} =𝔼⁡[|gℬ​(Z)−g⁡(Z)|]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[|g_{\mathcal{B}}(Z)-g(Z)|]
≤𝔼β⁡(g⁡(Z))[𝔼Z|β⁡(g⁡(Z))[|gℬ​(Z)−g⁡(Z)|]]\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\beta(g(Z))}\Big[\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{Z|\beta(g(Z))}[|g_{\mathcal{B}}(Z)-g(Z)|]\Big]
≤𝔼β⁡(g⁡(Z))[bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−1]\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\beta(g(Z))}\Big[b_{\beta(g(Z))}-b_{\beta(g(Z))-1}\Big]

We now use the fact that ℬ\mathcal{B} is α\alpha-well-balanced.

𝔼β⁡(g⁡(Z))[(bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−1)]\displaystyle\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\beta(g(Z))}\Big[(b_{\beta(g(Z))}-b_{\beta(g(Z))-1})\Big] =∑i=1Bℙ⁡(g⁡(Z)∈[bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−1,bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))])​(bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−1)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{B}\mathbb{P}\big(g(Z)\in[b_{\beta(g(Z))-1},b_{\beta(g(Z))}]\big)(b_{\beta(g(Z))}-b_{\beta(g(Z))-1})
≤∑i=1BαB​(bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−bβ⁡(g⁡(Z))−1)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{B}\frac{\alpha}{B}(b_{\beta(g(Z))}-b_{\beta(g(Z))-1})
≤αB\displaystyle\leq\frac{\alpha}{B}

Finally, from Lemma D.5, we get that MSE​(gℬ)≤MSE​(g)+2​αB\textup{MSE}(g_{\mathcal{B}})\leq\textup{MSE}(g)+\frac{2\alpha}{B}. ∎

The above lemma bounds the increase in MSE due to binning in the infinite sample case – next we deal with the finite sample case and prove proposition D.4:

Proof of Proposition D.4:

Ignoring all log\log factors, from Theorem D.2 if n=Ω~​(B)n=\widetilde{\Omega}(B), we have ‖g^ℬ−gℬ‖1=O⁡(1n​B)||\hat{g}_{\mathcal{B}}-g_{\mathcal{B}}||_{1}=O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{nB}}). Then from Lemma D.5, MSE​(g^ℬ)≤MSE​(gℬ)+O⁡(1B​n)≤MSE​(gℬ)+O⁡(1B)\textup{MSE}(\hat{g}_{\mathcal{B}})\leq\textup{MSE}(g_{\mathcal{B}})+O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{Bn}})\leq\textup{MSE}(g_{\mathcal{B}})+O(\frac{1}{B}). From Theorem D.6, since ℬ\mathcal{B} is 2-well-balanced, we have MSE​(gℬ)≤MSE​(g)+O⁡(1B)\textup{MSE}(g_{\mathcal{B}})\leq\textup{MSE}(g)+O(\frac{1}{B}). This gives us MSE​(g^ℬ)≤MSE​(g)+O⁡(1B)\textup{MSE}(\hat{g}_{\mathcal{B}})\leq\textup{MSE}(g)+O(\frac{1}{B}). ∎

D.3 Alternative binning schemes

We note that there are alternative binning schemes in the literature. For example, the BB bins can be chosen as I1=[0,1B],I2=(1B,2B],…,IB=(B−1B,1]I_{1}=[0,\frac{1}{B}],I_{2}=(\frac{1}{B},\frac{2}{B}],\dots,I_{B}=(\frac{B-1}{B},1]. The main problem with this binning scheme is that we may not be able to measure the calibration error efficiently, which is critical. However, if we choose the bins like this, and are lucky that the binning scheme happens to be 2-well-balanced, we can improve the bounds on the MSE that we proved above. This motivates alternative hybrid binning schemes, where we try to keep the width of the bins as close to 1/B1/B as possible, while ensuring that each bin contains lots of points as well. We think analyzing what binning schemes lead to the best bounds, and seeing if this can improve the calibration method, is a good direction for future research.

Appendix E Experimental details and ablations for section 4

We give more experimental details for our CIFAR-10 experiment, show experimental results for top-label calibration in ImageNet and CIFAR-10, and give details and results for our synthetic experiments. Note that the code is available in the supplementary folder for completeness.

Experimental details: We detail our experimental protocol for CIFAR-10 first. The CIFAR-10 validation set has 10,000 data points. We sampled, with replacement, a recalibration set of 1,000 points. In our theoretical approach and analysis, we split up these sets into multiple parts. For example, we used the first part for training a function, second part for bin construction, third part for binning. In practice, using the same set for all three steps worked out better, for both histogram binning and the scaling-binning calibrator. We believe that there may be theoretical justification for merging these sets, although we leave that for future work. For the marginal calibration experiment we ran either the scaling-binning calibrator (we fit a sigmoid in the function fitting step) or histogram binning. We calibrated each of the KK classes seprately as described in Section 2, and measured the marginal calibration error on the entire set of 10K points. We repeated this entire procedure 100 times, and computed mean and 90% confidence intervals.

In this experiment, we are checking a very precise hypothesis—assuming that the empirical distribution on the 10,000 validation points is the true data distribution, how do these methods perform? This is similar to the experimental protocol used in e.g. [18]. An alternative experimental protocol would have been to first split the CIFAR-10 data into two sets of size (1000,9000)(1000,9000). We could have then used the first set to recalibrate the model using either the scaling-binning calibrator or histogram binning, and then used the remaining 9,000 examples to estimate the calibration error on the ground truth distribution, using Bootstrap to compute confidence intervals. However, when we ran this experiment, we noticed that the results were very sensitive to which set of 1,000 points we used to recalibrate. Multiple runs of this experiment led to very different results. The point is that there are two sources of randomness—the randomness in the data the recalibration method operates on, and the randomness in the data used to evaluate and compare the recalibrators. In our protocol we account for both of these sources of randomness.

Top-label calibration experiments: We also ran experiments on top-label calibration, for both ImageNet and CIFAR-10. The protocol is exactly as described above, except instead of calibrating each of the KK classes, we calibrated the top probability prediction of the model. More concretely, for each input xix_{i}, the uncalibrated model outputs a probability pip_{i} corresponding to its top prediction kik_{i}, where the true label is yiy_{i}. We create a new dataset {(p1,𝕀⁡(k1=y1)),…,(pn,𝕀⁡(kn=yn))}\{(p_{1},\mathbb{I}(k_{1}=y_{1})),\dots,(p_{n},\mathbb{I}(k_{n}=y_{n}))\} and run the scaling-binning calibrator (fitting a sigmoid in the function fitting step, as in Platt scaling) or histogram binning on this dataset, using BB bins. This calibrates the probability corresponding to the top prediction of the model. We evaluate the recalibrated models on the top-label calibration error metric described in Section 2. For both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet we sampled, with replacement, a recalibration set of 1,000 points for the recalibration data, and we measured the calibration error on the entire set (10,000 points for CIFAR-10, and 50,000 points for ImageNet) as above. We show 90%90\% confidence intervals for all plots.

Figure 7(a) shows that on ImageNet the scaling-binning calibrator gets significantly lower calibration errors than histogram binning when B≥10B\geq 10, and nearly a 5 times lower calibration error when B=100B=100. Both methods get similar calibration errors when B=1B=1 or B=5B=5. Figure 7(b) shows that on CIFAR-10 when BB is high, the scaling-binning calibrator gets lower calibration errors than histogram binning, but when BB is low histogram binning gets lower calibration errors. We believe that the difference might be because the CIFAR-10 model is highly accurate at top-label prediction to begin with, getting an accuracy of over 93%93\%, so there is not much scope for re-calibration. In any case, this ablation tells us that practitioners should try multiple methods when recalibrating their models and evaluate their calibration error.

(A) Synthetic experiments to validate bounds: We first describe the scaling family we use, which is Platt scaling after applying a log-transform [12], otherwise known as beta calibration [52]. Let σ\sigma be the standard sigmoid function given by:

σ⁡(x)=11+exp⁡(−x)\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-x)}

Then, our recalibration family 𝒢\mathcal{G} consists of gg parameterized by a,ca,c, given by:

g⁡(z,a,c)=σ⁡(a​log⁡z1−z+c)g(z;a,c)=\sigma\Big(a\log{\frac{z}{1-z}}+c\Big)

In this set of synthetic experiments, we assume well-specification, that is P⁡(Y=1∣Z=z)=g⁡(z,a,c)P(Y=1\mid Z=z)=g(z;a,c) for some a,ca,c. We set P​(Z)=Uniform​[0,1]P(Z)=\mbox{Uniform}[0,1]. Since we know P⁡(Y=1∣Z)P(Y=1\mid Z), we can approximate the true squared calibration error in this case, even for scaling methods. To do this, we sample m=10000m=10000 points z1,…,zmz_{1},\dots,z_{m} independently from P⁡(Z)P(Z). An unbiased estimate of the squared calibration error then is:

(CE​(g))2≈1m​∑i=1m[P⁡(Y∣Z=zi)−g⁡(zi)]2(\textup{CE}(g))^{2}\approx\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big[P(Y\mid Z=z_{i})-g(z_{i})\big]^{2}

For each nn (number of recalibration samples) and BB (number of bins), we run either histogram binning or the scaling-binning calibrator with scaling family 𝒢\mathcal{G} and evaluate its calibration error as described above. We repeat this 1000 times, and compute 90% confidence intervals. We fix a=2a=2 and c=1c=1.

In the first sub-experiment we fix B=10B=10 and vary nn, plotting 1/ϵ21/\epsilon^{2} in Figure 8 (recall that ϵ2\epsilon^{2} is the squared calibration error). We plot the calibration errors for each method in a different plot because of the difference in scales, the scaling-binning calibrator achieves a much lower calibration error than histogram binning. As the theory predicts, we see that 1/ϵ21/\epsilon^{2} is approximately linear in nn for both calibrators. For example, when B=10B=10 if we increase from n=1000n=1000 to n=2000n=2000 the squared calibration error of histogram binning decreases by 2.00±0.062.00\pm 0.06 times, and the squared calibration error of our method decreases by 1.98±0.091.98\pm 0.09 times.

In the second sub-experiment we fix n=2000n=2000 and vary BB, plotting 1/ϵ21/\epsilon^{2} in Figure 11. For the scaling-binning calibrator 1/ϵ21/\epsilon^{2} is nearly constant (within the margin of error), but for histogram binning 1/ϵ21/\epsilon^{2} scales close to 1/B1/B. When n=2000n=2000 and we increase from 55 to 2020 bins, our method’s squared calibration error decreases by 2%±7%2\%\pm 7\% but for histogram binning it increases by 3.71±0.153.71\pm 0.15 times. For reference, we plot P⁡(Y∣Z=z)P(Y\mid Z=z) in Figure 10(a).

(B) Synthetic experiments to compare the scaling-binning calibrator and the scaling method: We run an illustrative toy experiment to show that there are some cases where the scaling-binning calibrator does better than the underlying scaling method—there are other cases where the underlying scaling method does better. the scaling-binning calibrator can do better because if we have infinite data, Proposition 3.3 showed that the binned version gℬg_{\mathcal{B}{}} has lower calibration error than gg. On the other hand, in step 3 of the scaling-binning calibrator algorithm we empirically bin the outputs of the scaling method which incurs an estimation error, and could mean the scaling-binning calibrator has higher calibration error than the underlying scaling method. Our key advantage is that unlike scaling methods our method has measurable calibration error so if we are not calibrated we can get more data or use a different scaling family.

Building on the previous synthetic experiments, in this experiment, we set the ground truth P⁡(Y=1∣Z=z)=g⁡(z,a,c)+h⁡(z)P(Y=1\mid Z=z)=g(z;a,c)+h(z) where for each zz, h⁡(z)∈{−0.02,0.02}h(z)\in\{-0.02,0.02\} with equal probability. In this case we set P​(Z)=Uniform​[0.25,0.75]P(Z)=\mbox{Uniform}[0.25,0.75] so that P⁡(Y=1∣Z=z)∈[0,1]P(Y=1\mid Z=z)\in[0,1]. We fix B=10B=10 and vary nn, plotting the squared calibration error ϵ2\epsilon^{2} in Figure 11. With B=10B=10 bins, n=3000n=3000 the squared calibration error is 5.2±1.15.2\pm 1.1 times lower for the scaling-binning calibrator than the underlying scaling method using a sigmoid recalibrator. For reference, we plot P⁡(Y∣Z=z)P(Y\mid Z=z) in Figure 10(b).

Appendix F Proofs for section 5

In this section we prove the finite sample bounds for the plugin and debiased estimators. We follow a very similar structure for both the plugin estimator and the debiased estimators.

We first give a proof for the plugin estimator. At a high level, we decompose the plugin estimator into three terms (Lemma F.2), and then bound each of these terms. Most of these terms simply involve algebraic manipulation and standard concentration results, except Lemma F.4 which requires some tricky conditioning.

The debiased estimator decomposes into three terms as well, two of these terms are the same as those in the plugin estimator. Bounding the third term (Lemma F.8) is the key to the improved sample complexity of the plugin estimator. The debiased estimator is not completely unbiased. However, with high probability if we condition on the xix_{i}s in the evaluation set, each of these error terms is unbiased. We can then use Hoeffding’s to concentrate each term near 0. The errors in each bin are then independent which leads to some cancelations of the error terms when we sum them up.

We use the following notation simplification to simplify the theorem statements and proofs:

pi=P⁡(f⁡(X)=si)p_{i}=P(f(X)=s_{i})
yi∗=𝔼⁡[Y|f⁡(X)=si]y_{i}^{*}=\mathbb{E}[Y\;|\;f(X)=s_{i}]
ei=(si−yi∗)e_{i}=(s_{i}-y_{i}^{*})

Then, if we let E∗2{E^{*}}^{2} denote the actual squared calibration error, we have:

E∗2=∑i=1bpi​ei2{E^{*}}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{b}p_{i}e_{i}^{2}

We begin by noting that pi^\hat{p_{i}} is close to pip_{i} for all ii. This is a standard application of either Bernstein’s inequality or the multiplicative Chernoff bound.

Lemma F.1.

Suppose pi>12n​log⁡2​Bδp_{i}>\frac{12}{n}\log{\frac{2B}{\delta}}{} for all ii. Then we can define c⁡(n)<0.5c(n)<0.5 such that except with probability δ\delta for all ii we have:

|pi^−pi|<c⁡(n)​pi:=3n​min⁡pi​log⁡2​Bδ​pi|\hat{p_{i}}-p_{i}|<c(n)p_{i}:=\sqrt{\frac{3}{n\min p_{i}}\log{\frac{2B}{\delta}}}p_{i}

F.1 Analysis of plugin estimator (proof of Theorem 5.3)

=∑i=1bpi^​[ei−(yi^−yi∗)]2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{b}\hat{p_{i}}[e_{i}-(\hat{y_{i}}-y_{i}^{*})]^{2}

In fact, we can also show that in the worst case the plugin estimator will need at least O⁡(Bϵ2)O(\frac{B}{\epsilon^{2}}) samples to estimate the calibration error. To see this, first note that the bias of the plugin estimator, which comes from term (P​3)(P3) is at least Bn\frac{B}{n}. So if n<0.1​Bϵ2n<0.1\frac{B}{\epsilon^{2}} we can consider very large BB, and use Chebyshev to show that that with high probability the estimation error is larger than ϵ2\epsilon^{2}.

F.2 Analysis of debiased estimator (proof of Theorem 5.4)

Next, we bound the error of the debiased estimator. The proof follows along the lines of the plugin estimator. We begin with a decomposition (Lemma F.7), similar to the decomposition of the plugin estimator. However, one of the terms in the decomposition, C​3C3, is different. Lemma F.8 bounds this term C​3C3. The rest of the proof is the same as for the plugin estimator, so we omit the other proofs.

As with the plugin estimator, we have a decomposition for the debiased estimator.

Lemma F.7 (Debiased decomposition).

The debiased estimator satisfies the following decomposition:

ℰ^db2=∑i=1bpi^​ei2⏟(C​1)−2​∑i=1bpi^​ei​(yi^−yi∗)⏟(C​2)+∑i=1bpi^​[(yi^−yi∗)2−yi^​(1−yi^)pi^​n−1]⏟(C​3)\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{db}}^{2}{}=\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{b}\hat{p_{i}}e_{i}^{2}}_{(C1)}-\underbrace{2\sum_{i=1}^{b}\hat{p_{i}}e_{i}(\hat{y_{i}}-y_{i}^{*})}_{(C2)}+\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{b}\hat{p_{i}}\Big[(\hat{y_{i}}-y_{i}^{*})^{2}-\frac{\hat{y_{i}}(1-\hat{y_{i}})}{\hat{p_{i}}n-1}\Big]}_{(C3)}

As with the plugin estimator, we bound each of the three terms. Notice that C​1C1 and C​2C2 are the same as terms P​1P1 and P​2P2 in the plugin estimator decomposition, so the bounds for those carry over. The next lemma bounds the error in C​3C3.

Lemma F.8.

Let (C​3)(C3) be as defined in Lemma F.7. Suppose |pi^−pi|<c⁡(n)​pi<0.5​pi|\hat{p_{i}}-p_{i}|<c(n)p_{i}<0.5p_{i} for all ii. Then with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta:

|(C​3)|≤3​Bn​log⁡nδ+δn|(C3)|\leq\frac{3\sqrt{B}}{n}\log{\frac{n}{\delta}}+\frac{\delta}{n}
Proof.

Let Z=(f⁡(x1),⋯,f⁡(xn))Z=(f(x_{1}),\cdots,f(x_{n})) be a random variable. We note that for all ii, pi^\hat{p_{i}} is a deterministic function of ZZ. For convenience, define tit_{i} as follows:

ti=(yi^−yi∗)2−yi^​(1−yi^)pi^​n−1t_{i}=(\hat{y_{i}}-y_{i}^{*})^{2}-\frac{\hat{y_{i}}(1-\hat{y_{i}})}{\hat{p_{i}}n-1}

Computing the expectation: The debiased estimator debiases the plugin estimator. In particular, we briefly explain why 𝔼[C​3∣Z]=0\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[C3\mid Z]=0. Since yi^\hat{y_{i}} is the mean of n​pi^n\hat{p_{i}} draws of a Bernoulli with parameter yi∗y_{i}^{*}, we have:

𝔼[(yi^−yi∗)2∣Z]=yi∗​(1−yi∗)n​pi^\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(\hat{y_{i}}-y_{i}^{*})^{2}\mid Z]=\frac{y_{i}^{*}(1-y_{i}^{*})}{n\hat{p_{i}}}

The term we subtracted is the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation of the samples, so from elementary statistics:

𝔼[yi^​(1−yi^)pi^​n−1∣Z]=yi∗​(1−yi∗)n​pi^\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\frac{\hat{y_{i}}(1-\hat{y_{i}})}{\hat{p_{i}}n-1}\mid Z\Big]=\frac{y_{i}^{*}(1-y_{i}^{*})}{n\hat{p_{i}}}

Which implies that 𝔼[C​3∣Z]=0\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[C3\mid Z]=0.

Bounding each term: By Hoeffding’s bound, for any fixed ii, we get that with probability at least 1−δn1-\frac{\delta}{n}:

|yi^−yi∗|≤12​pi^​n​log⁡2​nδ|\hat{y_{i}}-y_{i}^{*}|\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\hat{p_{i}}n}\log{\frac{2n}{\delta}}}

Let EiE_{i} be the event that this is indeed the case. Condition on EiE_{i} holding for all ii – by union bound this happens with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. With some algebra, we then get:

|pi^​ti|=|pi^​[(yi^−yi∗)2−yi^​(1−yi^)pi^​n−1]|≤32​n​log⁡Bδ\lvert\hat{p_{i}}t_{i}\rvert=\Big\lvert\hat{p_{i}}\Big[(\hat{y_{i}}-y_{i}^{*})^{2}-\frac{\hat{y_{i}}(1-\hat{y_{i}})}{\hat{p_{i}}n-1}\Big]\Big\rvert\leq\frac{3}{2n}\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}

Concentration: Next, we analyze the concentration of T=[(C3)∣Z,∀i.Ei]T=\big[(C3)\mid Z,\forall i.E_{i}\big] around its mean μ\mu. |pi^​ti|\lvert\hat{p_{i}}t_{i}\rvert is bounded so is sub-Gaussian with parameter:

σi2=94​n2​log⁡Bδ\sigma_{i}^{2}=\frac{9}{4n^{2}}\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}

Each term pi^​ti\hat{p_{i}}t_{i} in the sum is independent, even when conditioned on ZZ. So TT is sub-Gaussian with parameter:

σ2=∑i=1Bσi2=9​B4​n2​log⁡Bδ\sigma^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sigma_{i}^{2}=\frac{9B}{4n^{2}}\log{\frac{B}{\delta}}

|T−μ|≤2​σ2​log⁡1δ≤3​22​Bn​log⁡nδ​log⁡1δ\lvert T-\mu\rvert\leq\sqrt{2\sigma^{2}\log{\frac{1}{\delta}}}\leq\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\frac{\sqrt{B}}{n}\sqrt{\log{\frac{n}{\delta}}\log{\frac{1}{\delta}}}

This can be simplified to:

|T−μ|≤3​Bn​log⁡nδ\lvert T-\mu\rvert\leq\frac{3\sqrt{B}}{n}\log{\frac{n}{\delta}}

Bounding the bias: Although 𝔼[C​3∣Z]=0\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[C3\mid Z]=0, conditioning on EiE_{i} introduces some bias. However, we can show this bias is small. First, notice that |ti|≤1|t_{i}|\leq 1. The event EiE_{i} holds with probability at least 1−δn1-\frac{\delta}{n}. Then by the law of total expectation, conditioning on EiE_{i} shifts the mean by at most δn\frac{\delta}{n} – in other words |𝔼[ti∣Ei,Z]|≤δn|\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[t_{i}\mid E_{i},Z]|\leq\frac{\delta}{n}. Summing over tit_{i}s, we get:

|𝔼[(C3)∣Z,∀i.Ei]|≤∑i=1Bpi^|𝔼[ti∣Ei,Z]|≤δn\lvert\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(C3)\mid Z,\forall i.E_{i}]\rvert\leq\sum_{i=1}^{B}\hat{p_{i}}\lvert\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[t_{i}\mid E_{i},Z]\rvert\leq\frac{\delta}{n}

Finishing up: Combining the bias and concentration, we get that with probability at least 1−2​δ1-2\delta:

|(C​3)|≤3​Bn​log⁡nδ+δn|(C3)|\leq\frac{3\sqrt{B}}{n}\log{\frac{n}{\delta}}+\frac{\delta}{n}

∎

We combine the bounds for (C​1)(C1), (C​2)(C2), (C​3)(C3), as in Theorem F.6, to bound the estimation error of the debiased estimator.

Theorem F.9.

In the same setting as Theorem F.6, for the debiased estimator, with probability at least 1−4​δ1-4\delta,

|E^2−E∗2|≤c⁡(n)​E∗2+2​(1+c⁡(n))​E∗2n​log⁡2δ+3​Bn​log⁡nδ+δn|\hat{E}^{2}-{E^{*}}^{2}|\leq c(n){E^{*}}^{2}+\sqrt{\frac{2(1+c(n)){E^{*}}^{2}}{n}\log{\frac{2}{\delta}}}+\frac{3\sqrt{B}}{n}\log{\frac{n}{\delta}}+\frac{\delta}{n}

We interpret the bound in Theorem F.9 in two regimes. In the first regime, we fix the problem parameters pi,E∗2p_{i},{E^{*}}^{2}, and look at what happens as we send nn to infinity. In that case, the second term dominates, and we see that the error is approximately proportional to 1n\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}, which is the same as for the plugin estimator. However, in general we do not need to estimate the calibration error extremely finely, and may be satisfied as long as we estimate the calibration error within a constant multiplicative factor. That is, we might only need nn to be large enough so that our estimate E^2\hat{E}^{2} is on the right order, e.g. between 0.5​E∗20.5{E^{*}}^{2} and 1.5​E∗21.5{E^{*}}^{2} (where 0.50.5 and 1.51.5 can be replaced by other constants). In that regime, the third term dominates and the error is approximately proportional to Bn\frac{\sqrt{B}}{n}, which is better than for the plugin estimator where it is proportional to Bn\frac{B}{n} (see Theorem F.6). This is captured in the final bound, where the proof closely parallels that of Theorem 5.3.

Restatement of Theorem 5.4.

Suppose we have a binned model with squared calibration error ℰ2\mathcal{E}^{2}{} and for all s∈Ss\in S, ℙ⁡(f⁡(X)=s)≥12​B\mathbb{P}(f(X)=s)\geq\frac{1}{2B}. If n≥c​Bℰ2​log⁡Bδn\geq c\frac{\sqrt{B}}{\mathcal{E}^{2}{}}\log{\frac{B}{\delta}} for some universal constant cc then for the debiased estimator, we have 12​ℰ2≤ℰ^db2≤32​ℰ2\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}{}\leq\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{db}}^{2}{}\leq\frac{3}{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}{} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Appendix G Additional experiments for section 5

G.1 Debiasing the ECE

We propose a way to more accurately estimate the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error (popularly known as ECE), and run experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 that show that we can estimate the error much better than prior work, which uses the plugin estimator. The key insight is the same as for the ℓ2\ell_{2} calibration error—the plugin estimator for the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error is biased and this bias leads to inaccurate estimates. To estimate the error better we can subtract an approximation of the bias which leads to a better estimate. The main difference is that for the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error we were not able to approximate the bias with a closed form expression and instead use a Gaussian approximation.

Recall that the ℓ1​-CE\ell_{1}\textup{-CE}{} is the ℓp\ell_{p}{} calibration error with p=1p=1, redefined below:

Definition G.1.

The ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error of f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] is given by:

ℓ1​-CE​(f)=𝔼[|f⁡(X)−𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)]|]\displaystyle\ell_{1}\textup{-CE}(f)=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\big[\left|f(X)-\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)]\right|\big] (7)

Estimating the ℓ1​-CE\ell_{1}\textup{-CE}{} for many models is challenging (see Section 3) so prior work instead selects a binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{} and estimates ℓ1​-CE​(fℬ)\ell_{1}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}}) of a model ff. Suppose we wish to measure the binned calibration error ℰ=ℓ1​-CE​(fℬ)\mathcal{E}{}=\ell_{1}\textup{-CE}(f_{\mathcal{B}{}}) of a model f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] where |ℬ|=B|\mathcal{B}{}|=B. Suppose we get an evaluation set Tn={(x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)}T_{n}=\{(x_{1},y_{1}),\dots,(x_{n},y_{n})\}. Past work typically estimates the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error using a plugin estimate for each term:

Definition G.2 (Plugin estimator for ℓ1​-CE\ell_{1}\textup{-CE}{}).

Let LkL_{k} denote the data points where the model outputs a prediction in the kk-th bin of ℬ\mathcal{B}{}: Lk={(xj,yj)∈Tn|f⁡(xj)∈Ik}L_{k}=\{(x_{j},y_{j})\in T_{n}\;|\;f(x_{j})\in I_{k}\}.

Let p^k\hat{p}_{k} be the estimated probability of ff outputting a prediction in the kk-th bin: p^k=|Lk|n\hat{p}_{k}=\frac{|L_{k}|}{n}.

Let y^k\hat{y}_{k} be the empirical average of YY in the kk-th bin: y^k=∑x,y∈Lky|Lk|\hat{y}_{k}=\sum_{x,y\in L_{k}}\frac{y}{|L_{k}|}.

Let s^k\hat{s}_{k} be the empirical average of the model outputs in the kk-th bin: s^k=∑x,y∈Lkf⁡(x)|Lk|\hat{s}_{k}=\sum_{x,y\in L_{k}}\frac{f(x)}{|L_{k}|}.

The plugin estimate for the binned ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error is the weighted squared difference between y^k\hat{y}_{k} and s^k\hat{s}_{k}:

ℰ^pl=∑k=1Bp^k​|s^k−y^k|\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{}=\sum_{k=1}^{B}\hat{p}_{k}\lvert\hat{s}_{k}-\hat{y}_{k}\rvert

The plugin estimate is a biased estimate of the binned calibration error. Intuitively, this is because of the absolute value: on any finite samples sks_{k} and yky_{k} will differ and the absolute value of the difference will be positive, even if the population values are the same. More concretely consider a model ff where 𝔼[f⁡(X)∣f⁡(X)∈Ik]=𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)∈Ik]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[f(X)\mid f(X)\in I_{k}]=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)\in I_{k}] in every bin kk. In that case the binned calibration error ℰ\mathcal{E}{} is 00. But on any finite samples the plugin estimate ℰ^pl\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{} will be larger than 00. In particular, the plugin estimator overestimates the binned calibration error, and the extent of overestimation may be different for different models.

To improve the estimate, we can subtract an approximation of the bias. That is, we would like to output ℰ^pl−(𝔼[ℰ^pl]−ℰ)\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{}-(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{}]-\mathcal{E}{}) as our estimate of the calibration error, where 𝔼[ℰ^pl]−ℰ\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{}]-\mathcal{E}{} is the bias. However, 𝔼[ℰ^pl]−ℰ\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{}]-\mathcal{E}{} is difficult to approximate in closed form. Instead, we propose approximating it by simulating draws from a normal approximation. More precisely, let yk=𝔼[Y∣f⁡(X)∈Ik]y_{k}=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid f(X)\in I_{k}]. Then, each label in the kk-th bin is a draw from a Bernoulli distribution with parameter yky_{k}. So y^k\hat{y}_{k} is the mean of n​p^kn\hat{p}_{k} Bernoulli draws. Assuming that the number of points in each bin is not too small, we can approximate y^k\hat{y}_{k} using a Gaussian approximation, and use that to approximate the bias 𝔼[ℰ^pl]−ℰ\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{}]-\mathcal{E}{}.

Definition G.3 (Debiased estimator for ℓ1​-CE\ell_{1}\textup{-CE}{}).

For each kk, let RkR_{k} be a random variable sampled from a normal approximation of the label distribution in the kk-th bin: Rk∼N⁡(y^k,y^k​(1−y^k)n​p^k)R_{k}\sim N(\hat{y}_{k},\frac{\hat{y}_{k}(1-\hat{y}_{k})}{n\hat{p}_{k}}). The debiased estimate for the binned ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error subtracts an approximation of the bias from the plugin estimate:

ℰ^db=ℰ^pl−(𝔼[∑k=1Bp^k​|s^k−Rk|]−ℰ^pl)\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{db}}{}=\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{}-(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{B}\hat{p}_{k}\lvert\hat{s}_{k}-R_{k}\rvert\Big]-\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\textup{pl}}{})

We can approximate the expectation in the debiased estimator by simulating many draws from a normal distribution, which is computationally fairly inexpensive. Note that our proposed estimator is a heuristic approach, and future work should examine whether we can get provably better estimation rates for estimating the ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error, as we did for the ℓ2\ell_{2} calibration error. That might involve analyzing our proposed estimator, or may involve coming up with a completely different estimator.

We run multiclass top-label calibration experiment on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet which suggests that the debiased estimator produces better estimates of the calibration error than the plugin estimator. We describe the protocol for ImageNet first, which is similar to the experimental protocol in Section 5.1. We split the validation set of size 50,000 into two sets SCS_{C}{} and SES_{E}{} of sizes 3,000 and 47,000 respectively. Note that a practitioner would not need so many data points when estimating their model’s calibration, we use 47,000 points only so that we can reliably compare the estimators. We use SCS_{C}{} to re-calibrate a trained VGG-16 model and select a binning scheme ℬ\mathcal{B}{} so that each bin contains an equal number of points (uniform-mass binning). We calibrate the top probability prediction as described in Section 2 using Platt scaling. For varying values of nn, we sample nn points with replacement from SES_{E}{}, and estimate the binned ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error (ECE) using the plugin estimator and our proposed debiased estimator. We used B=100B=100 or B=15B=15 bins in our experiments. We then compute the squared deviation of these estimates from the binned ℓ1\ell_{1} calibration error measured on the entire set SES_{E}{}. We repeat this resampling 1,000 times to get the mean squared deviation of the estimates from the ground truth and 90% confidence intervals. Figure 12 shows that the debiased estimates are much closer to the ground truth than the plugin estimates—the difference is especially significant when the number of samples nn is small or the number of bins BB is large. Note that having a perfect estimate corresponds to 00 on the vertical axis.

For CIFAR-10 we use the same protocol except we split the validation set of size 10,000 into two sets SCS_{C}{} and SES_{E}{} of sizes 3,000 and 7,000 respectively. Figure 4(a) shows that the debiased estimates are much closer to the ground truth than the plugin estimates in this case as well.

G.2 Additional experiments for estimating calibration error

In Section 5 we ran an experiment on CIFAR-10 to show that the debiased estimator gives estimates closer to the true calubration error than the plugin estimator. To give more insight into this, Figure 14 shows a histogram of the absolute difference between the estimates and ground truth for the plugin and debiased estimator, over the 1,000 resamples, when we use B=10B=10 or B=100B=100 bins. For B=10B=10 bins it is not completely clear which estimator is doing better but the debiased estimator avoids very bad estimates. However, when B=100B=100, the debiased estimator produces estimates much closer to the ground truth (00 on the x-axis).

We also show histograms for the ECE experiments in Appendix G.1, in Figure 15 for ImageNet and Figure 16 for CIFAR-10. These histograms show that the proposed debiased estimator produces estimates much closer to the ground truth than the plugin estimator.

We also ran a marginal multiclass calibration experiment on CIFAR-10 to show that our estimator allows us to select models with a lower mean-squared error subject to a given calibration constraint. In this case we split the validation set into SCS_{C}{} and SES_{E}{} of size 6000 and 4000 respectively, and recalibrated a trained model on SCS_{C}{}. On SES_{E}{}, we estimate the calibration error using the plugin and debiased estimators and use 100 Bootstrap resamples to compute a 90% upper confidence bound on the estimate (from the variance of the Bootstrap samples). We compute the mean-squared error and the upper bounds on the calibration error for B=10,15,…,100B=10,15,\dots,100 and show the Pareto curve in Figure 17. Figure 17 shows that for any desired calibration error, the debiased estimator enables us to pick out models with a better mean-squared error. For example, if we want a model with calibration error less than 1.5%1.5\%, the debiased estimator tells us we can confidently use 100 bins, while relying on the plugin estimator only lets us use 15 bins and incurs a 13% higher mean-squared error.
